knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial and quadratic 0-1 programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial 0-1, pseudo-Boolean, and quadratic 0-1 models by the forms of their objective and constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonlinear $0$-$1$ program is called a polynomial $0$-$1$ programming problem, or a pseudo-Boolean optimization problem, when its objective $f$ and every constraint function $g_i$ have the multilinear form $\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_jx_j+\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_k\prod_{i\in S(k)}x_i$, with $|S(k)|\ge 2$ for every nonlinear monomial. If $f$ and every $g_i$ instead have the quadratic form $\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_jx_j+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}x_ix_j$, the problem is called a quadratic $0$-$1$ programming problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear 0-1 program is polynomial 0-1 programming, also called pseudo-Boolean optimization, when its objective and all constraint functions are multilinear polynomials of the displayed form. When every such function contains only linear and pairwise-product terms, it is quadratic 0-1 programming.
assumptions_latex: \text{The objective }f\text{ and every constraint function }g_i\text{ have the stated multilinear form.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The problem is polynomial }0\text{-}1\text{ programming, also called pseudo-Boolean optimization; if every function has the stated quadratic form, it is quadratic }0\text{-}1\text{ programming.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit quartic and sextic minimum-volume sublevel sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The prescribed set \(K\) and problem \(\mathbf P\) retain their definitions from the surrounding formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[g_4(x)=x_1^4+x_2^4-x_1^2x_2^2,\qquad G_1^4=\{x:g_4(x)\leq1\},\] and \[g_6(x)=x_1^6+x_2^6-\tfrac12\bigl(x_1^4x_2^2+x_1^2x_2^4\bigr),\qquad G_1^6=\{x:g_6(x)\leq1\}.\] Then \(G_1^4\) is the unique solution of problem \(\mathbf P\) for \(d=4\): \(K\subset G_1^4\), and \(G_1^4\) has minimum volume among the sets containing \(K\) that are defined by homogeneous polynomials of degree four. Likewise, \(G_1^6\) is the unique solution of \(\mathbf P\) for \(d=6\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed quartic and sextic homogeneous polynomials define the unique optimal containing sublevel sets for the surrounding minimum-volume problem in degrees four and six, respectively.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_1^4\text{ is the unique solution of }\mathbf P\text{ for }d=4,\qquad G_1^6\text{ is the unique solution of }\mathbf P\text{ for }d=6

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Molecular distance geometry and its zero-residual formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines three-dimensional distance realization and its equivalent zero-residual polynomial formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(S\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}\) and distances \(d_{ij}\ge 0\) for \(\{i,j\}\in S\), the molecular distance geometry problem seeks \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^3\) such that \(\|x_i-x_j\|=d_{ij}\) for all \(\{i,j\}\in S\). Define \[f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in S}\left(\|x_i-x_j\|^2-d_{ij}^2\right)^2.\] Then the distance constraints hold if and only if \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The molecular distance geometry problem seeks three-dimensional atom positions realizing specified nonnegative interatomic distances. A configuration realizes every specified distance exactly if and only if the associated sum of squared errors in squared distances is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall\{i,j\}\in S,\ \|x_i-x_j\|=d_{ij}\right)\iff f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Box-Constrained Polynomial Optimization Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial optimization on a nonnegative box, with the approximation claim interpreted as uniform approximation of continuous problem data rather than automatic convergence of feasible sets, minimizers, or optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R_+^n\) with \(a\le b\) componentwise. A box-constrained polynomial optimization problem has the form
\[
\min\left\{f_0(x)\mid f_i(x)\ge 0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ a\le x\le b\right\},
\]
where, for each \(i=0,\ldots,m\),
\[
f_i(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A_i}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha,\qquad x^\alpha=\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\alpha_j},
\]
with finite \(A_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_+^n\) and \(c_{i\alpha}\in\mathbb R\). Because polynomials are dense in \(C([a,b])\) under the supremum norm, finitely many continuous objective and constraint functions on the box can be uniformly approximated arbitrarily closely by polynomial data. The problem family contains NP-hard special cases, including nonconvex quadratic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-constrained polynomial optimization problem minimizes a polynomial objective over a nonnegative box subject to finitely many polynomial inequalities. Each polynomial is a finite real linear combination of monomials with nonnegative integer exponents. Polynomial density gives arbitrary uniform approximation of continuous objective and constraint data on the box; by itself, it does not guarantee convergence of feasible sets or solutions. The family includes NP-hard cases such as nonconvex quadratic optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{f_0(x)\mid f_i(x)\ge0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ a\le x\le b\}\text{ is a box-constrained polynomial optimization problem; polynomial data uniformly approximate continuous data on }[a,b]\text{, and the family contains NP-hard special cases.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonally constrained QCQP, relative-range maximizers, and homogenization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the problem family and its approximation metric. The relative-range ratio requires a nonzero objective range; the extract supplies no convention for the constant-objective case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathcal S^n\), \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), and define \(\mathcal F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j^2=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ \sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_j^2\le d_i\ (i=1,\ldots,p)\}\). When \(\mathcal F\) is nonempty and bounded, set \(\bar q(Q)=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}x^TQx\) and \(\underline q(Q)=\min_{x\in\mathcal F}x^TQx\). If \(\bar q(Q)>\underline q(Q)\), an \(\epsilon\)-maximizer, \(\epsilon\in[0,1]\), is an \(x\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(\frac{\bar q(Q)-x^TQx}{\bar q(Q)-\underline q(Q)}\le\epsilon\). Moreover, \(\max_{x\in\mathcal F}(x^TQx+\ell^Tx)\) is value-equivalent to \(\max\{x^TQx+t\ell^Tx:x\in\mathcal F,\ t^2=1\}\), with recovery \(x' = tx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonally constrained QCQP optimizes a quadratic form over equality and inequality constraints in the coordinate squares. On a nonempty bounded feasible set, an epsilon-maximizer has relative loss at most epsilon compared with the full objective range. A linear objective term can be homogenized by adjoining a sign variable t with t squared equal to one; the original optimizer is recovered as t times x.
assumptions_latex: \bar q(Q)>\underline q(Q)\text{ for the relative-range definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\bar q(Q)-x^TQx}{\bar q(Q)-\underline q(Q)}\le\epsilon,\qquad \max_{x\in\mathcal F}(x^TQx+\ell^Tx)=\max_{x\in\mathcal F,\ t^2=1}(x^TQx+t\ell^Tx).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence, uniqueness, and contact-measure optimality conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the convex problem \(\mathcal P\) defined in the surrounding polynomial sublevel-set formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact with nonempty interior. Then \(\mathcal P\) has a unique optimal solution \(g^*\in\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d\). If \(g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d)\), there exists \(\mu^*\in\mathcal M(K)_+\) such that, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb N^n\) with \(|\alpha|=d\), \[\int_{\mathbb R^n}x^\alpha e^{-g^*(x)}\,dx=\int_Kx^\alpha\,d\mu^*,\] and \[\int_K(1-g^*)\,d\mu^*=0,\qquad \mu^*(K)=\frac nd\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-g^*(x)}\,dx.\] The measure is supported on \(V=\{x\in K:g^*(x)=1\}\) and may be replaced by a positive measure supported on at most \(\binom{n+d-1}{d}\) points of \(V\). Conversely, if \(g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d)\), \(1-g^*\in C_d(K)\), and there are \(x(i)\in K\) and \(\lambda_i>0\) satisfying \(g^*(x(i))=1\) and \[\int_{\mathbb R^n}x^\alpha e^{-g^*(x)}\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^s\lambda_i x(i)^\alpha\qquad(|\alpha|=d),\] then \(g^*\) is the unique optimal solution of \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compact K with nonempty interior, the convex sublevel-set problem has a unique optimizer. An interior optimizer has a positive contact-measure certificate matching all degree-d moments, and the certificate can use at most binomial(n+d−1,d) contact points. Conversely, feasible positive contact weights satisfying those moment equations certify unique optimality.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is the convex problem defined in the surrounding formulation}
g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d)\text{ for the contact-measure conclusion}
g^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbf P[\mathbf x]_d),\ 1-g^*\in C_d(K),\ g^*(x(i))=1,\ \lambda_i>0\text{ for the converse}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\text{ has a unique optimizer; under the stated interior condition it admits the displayed contact-measure certificate, and the stated finite contact-point conditions imply unique optimality}

knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Unconstrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained global minimization of a real polynomial in one scalar variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[t]\), the univariate unconstrained polynomial model has extended-real optimal value \[p^*:=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}p(t).\] The model is bounded below exactly when \(p^*>-\infty\). In that case the infimum is attained and the nonempty solution set is \[X^*:=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:p(t)=p^*\}.\] Otherwise \(p^*=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a real polynomial over the entire real line. Its infimum is either negative infinity or a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}p(t)\), with attainment whenever \(p^*>-\infty\)

notation.meaning: extended-real global infimum of the polynomial
set of global minimizers when the polynomial is bounded below

knowledge_statements.title: Multivariate Unconstrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained global minimization of a real polynomial in finitely many variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the multivariate unconstrained polynomial model is \[f^*:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x).\] Its global minimizers form \(X^*:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)=f^*\}\) when \(f^*\) is finite and attained. No convexity, coercivity, or boundedness assumption is implicit in this problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a real multivariate polynomial over all Euclidean space, without assuming convexity, boundedness, or attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Unconstrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling classification for unconstrained minimization of a homogeneous polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be homogeneous of positive degree \(d\), so \(f(\lambda x)=\lambda^d f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&f(x)\geq0\text{ for all }x,\\-\infty,&f(u)<0\text{ for some }u.\end{cases}\] In the first case the origin is a global minimizer; in the second, \(f(\lambda u)\to-\infty\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-degree homogeneity forces the unconstrained infimum to be zero for a nonnegative form and negative infinity if any negative value exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\in\{0,-\infty\}\), classified by global nonnegativity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constrained global minimization, feasibility, and minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the general mixed equality–inequality problem and both global and local solution concepts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m, let f,g_i,h_j:X\to\mathbb{R}, and define D=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le 0\ (i=1,\ldots,k),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=k+1,\ldots,r)\}. The constrained global minimum is f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x), when attained, and the global-minimizer set is X^*=\{x\in D:f(x)=f^*\}. A point x\in D is a local minimizer if \exists\epsilon>0\ \forall y\in D,\ \|y-x\|<\epsilon\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible set consists of points satisfying every inequality and equality constraint. The global problem seeks the attained minimum value and all feasible points attaining it. A feasible point is a local minimizer when its objective value is no larger than that of every sufficiently close feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x),\quad X^*=\{x\in D:f(x)=f^*\},\quad x\text{ local}\iff x\in D\land\exists\epsilon>0\ \forall y\in D:\|y-x\|<\epsilon\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT triplet and associated shifted Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT definition for polynomial inequality and equality constraints, using the source's sign convention and subtraction of the global optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A triplet (x^*,\lambda^*,v^*)\in K	imes\mathbb R^{m_1}	imes\mathbb R^{m_2} is a KKT triplet if 
abla f(x^*)=\sum_{j=1}^{m_1}\lambda_j^*
abla g_j(x^*)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_2}v_\ell^*
abla h_\ell(x^*), \lambda_j^*g_j(x^*)=0, and \lambda_j^*\ge0 for every j. Its associated Lagrangian is L(x,\lambda^*,v^*)=f(x)-f^*-\sum_{j=1}^{m_1}\lambda_j^*g_j(x)-\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_2}v_\ell^*h_\ell(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and multiplier vectors form a KKT triplet when stationarity, complementary slackness, and nonnegativity of inequality multipliers hold. The associated shifted Lagrangian subtracts the optimal value and the multiplier-weighted constraints from the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
abla f(x^*)=\sum_j\lambda_j^*
abla g_j(x^*)+\sum_\ell v_\ell^*
abla h_\ell(x^*),\quad \lambda_j^*g_j(x^*)=0,\quad\lambda_j^*\ge0,\quad L=f-f^*-\sum_j\lambda_j^*g_j-\sum_\ell v_\ell^*h_\ell.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient upper bound and variable-fixation penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For maximization of a multilinear polynomial over binary variables; the displayed extrema are understood where their indexing sets are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{p}c_k\prod_{j\in S_k}x_j\), \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), define \(\bar z_1=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\max\{0,c_k\}\) and \(T^{-1}(j)=\{k:j\in S_k\}\). The loss in this bound caused by fixing \(x_j=0\) is bounded below by \(p_j^0=\sum_{k\in T^{-1}(j)}\max\{0,c_k\}\). For fixing \(x_j=1\), define \(p_j^1=-\min_{S_k=\{j\}}\{0,c_k\}+\sum_{(k,k')}\min\{|c_k|,|c_{k'}|\}\), where the sum ranges over pairs satisfying \(S_k=\{l\}\), \(S_{k'}=\{l,j\}\), and \(c_kc_{k'}<0\). These penalties may be subtracted from \(\bar z_1\) after the corresponding fixation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polynomial objective in binary variables, the sum of all positive monomial coefficients is an upper bound. Fixing a variable to zero removes every positive-coefficient term containing it, giving the zero-fixation penalty. Fixing it to one permits deductions from negative singleton terms and cancellation between opposite-sign linear and associated bilinear terms, giving the one-fixation penalty. The applicable penalty can be subtracted to tighten the bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar z_1=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\max\{0,c_k\}\text{ is an upper bound, and fixing }x_j=a\text{ permits the deduction }p_j^a\text{ for }a\in\{0,1\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Revised Taha's Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-level search algorithm for the constrained polynomial 0–1 problem denoted by \((0\text{-}1PP_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(J_0=\varnothing\), \(t=0\), and \(f_{\mathrm{opt}}=\infty\). At \(J_t\), apply the modified additive algorithm to \((MP_t)\) to seek a feasible partial solution \(J_t^*\subseteq\bar I_t\) with objective value strictly below \(f_{\mathrm{opt}}\), augmenting \(J_t\) when one is found and otherwise fathoming by feasibility. Fathom inconsistent \(J_t\) by consistency; otherwise construct \(D_t\). If \(B_t=\varnothing\), set \(y^*=y^t\) and \(f_{\mathrm{opt}}=\widetilde f^t\) and fathom by optimality; otherwise append \(B_t\) to \(J_t\). Fathom by domination when \(\widetilde f^t\ge f_{\mathrm{opt}}\). If \(\widetilde g_i^t(y^t)\le b_i\) for every \(i\in M\), update \(y^*=y^t\) and \(f_{\mathrm{opt}}=\widetilde f^t\) and fathom by optimality; otherwise set \(J_{t+1}=J_t\), increment \(t\), and repeat. During backtracking, stop if every element of \(J_t\) is underlined; otherwise replace the rightmost non-underlined element by its underlined complement, delete all elements to its right, increment \(t\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method searches over partial binary solutions, fathoming them by infeasibility, inconsistency, domination, or optimality. It updates the incumbent when the polynomial constraints are satisfied and backtracks by complementing the rightmost non-underlined choice and deleting subsequent choices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The resulting procedure is a partial-solution search with feasibility, consistency, domination, and optimality fathoming and complement-based backtracking.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Penalty-improved upper bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the coefficient upper bound and the two fixation penalties defined for each binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar z_1\) be an upper bound for \(f\), and let \(p_j^0,p_j^1\) be valid deductions from that bound when \(x_j\) is fixed to \(0\) or \(1\), respectively. Then \[\bar z_2=\bar z_1-\max_{j=1,\ldots,n}\min\{p_j^0,p_j^1\}\] is a valid improved upper bound for \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every binary variable, take the smaller of the valid bound reductions obtained from its two possible fixings. Subtracting the largest such guaranteed reduction from the original bound produces another valid, no-weaker upper bound.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\leq \bar z_2=\bar z_1-\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\min\{p_j^0,p_j^1\}\leq \bar z_1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Penalty-based branch-and-bound for constrained polynomial 0-1 optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The fixation variable is written consistently as \(x_j\); this normalizes apparent index slips in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constrained polynomial maximization problem over \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize a feasible incumbent \((x_{\mathrm{opt}},f_{\mathrm{opt}})\). At each node compute a valid objective upper bound \(\bar f\); fathom the node if \(\bar f\leq f_{\mathrm{opt}}\). Update the incumbent whenever a better feasible point is found. For every constraint \(g_i(x)\leq b_i\), fathom the node if a valid lower bound \(L_i>b_i\). For each free \(x_j\), fix \(x_j=1\) if \(\bar f-p_j^0\leq f_{\mathrm{opt}}\), and fix \(x_j=0\) if \(\bar f-p_j^1\leq f_{\mathrm{opt}}\). Likewise, fix \(x_j=1\) if \(L_i+p_{ij}^0>b_i\), and fix \(x_j=0\) if \(L_i+p_{ij}^1>b_i\). Rebound after any fixation; otherwise branch into \(x_j=0\) and \(x_j=1\), and continue until no live node remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a feasible incumbent. Prune a node when its objective upper bound cannot beat the incumbent or when a constraint lower bound proves infeasibility. Use objective and constraint penalties to eliminate one value of a free binary variable whenever that value cannot improve the incumbent or cannot satisfy a constraint. If no fixation applies, branch on a free variable and continue until all live subproblems have been processed.
assumptions_latex: \bar f\text{ is a valid node upper bound on the maximization objective}
L_i\text{ is a valid node lower bound on }g_i
p_j^0,p_j^1,p_{ij}^0,p_{ij}^1\text{ are valid conditional bound penalties}
\text{node selection and backtracking exhaust all unfathomed subproblems}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{When no live node remains, }x_{\mathrm{opt}}\text{ is globally optimal for the polynomial 0-1 program.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truncated Tangency Variety
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the polynomial radial-dependence equations and their intersection with a nonempty attained sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]\). For \(1\le i<j\le n\), define
\[
g_{ij}(\mathbf x)=x_j\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf x)-x_i\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}(\mathbf x).
\]
For an attained value \(M\in f(\mathbb R^n)\), the truncated tangency variety is
\[
\Gamma_M(f)=\left\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n: f(\mathbf x)\le M,\ g_{ij}(\mathbf x)=0\ \text{for every }1\le i<j\le n\right\}.
\]
The equations state that \(\mathbf x\) and \(\nabla f(\mathbf x)\) are linearly dependent; at regular nonzero points this expresses tangency between a level set of \(f\) and the centered sphere through \(\mathbf x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The truncated tangency variety is the attained sublevel set where the position vector and polynomial gradient are linearly dependent. At regular nonzero points, this is the locus where an objective level set is tangent to the centered sphere through the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma_M(f)=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n:f(\mathbf x)\le M,\ x_j\partial_i f(\mathbf x)-x_i\partial_j f(\mathbf x)=0\ \forall i<j\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of the Global Infimum to the Truncated Tangency Variety
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States exact equality of the unrestricted polynomial infimum and the infimum over the associated truncated tangency set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]\), let \(M\in f(\mathbb R^n)\), define
\[
g_{ij}(\mathbf x)=x_j\partial_i f(\mathbf x)-x_i\partial_j f(\mathbf x),
\]
and set
\[
\Gamma_M(f)=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n:f(\mathbf x)\le M,\ g_{ij}(\mathbf x)=0\ \text{for all }i<j\}.
\]
Then
\[
\inf_{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n}f(\mathbf x)=\inf_{\mathbf x\in\Gamma_M(f)}f(\mathbf x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any attained level M, restricting a polynomial objective to its truncated radial tangency locus does not change its global infimum.
assumptions_latex: \Gamma_M(f)=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n:f(\mathbf x)\le M,\ x_j\partial_i f(\mathbf x)-x_i\partial_j f(\mathbf x)=0\ \forall i<j\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n}f(\mathbf x)=\inf_{\mathbf x\in\Gamma_M(f)}f(\mathbf x).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Finite Real Varieties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and enumeration characterization when the real variety has finitely many points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,h_1,\ldots,h_m\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and suppose the real variety \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)=\{v^{(1)},\ldots,v^{(N)}\}\) is nonempty and finite. Then the polynomial optimization problem over this variety attains its minimum and \[f^*=\min_{1\leq k\leq N}f\bigl(v^{(k)}\bigr),\qquad X^*=\left\{v^{(k)}:f\bigl(v^{(k)}\bigr)=f^*\right\}.\] Thus the optimizer set is also nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonempty finite real variety, every polynomial attains its minimum, obtained by comparing its values at all feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\min_{v\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(v)\) and \(X^*\neq\varnothing\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic and Basic Closed Semialgebraic Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial sign-condition presentations in real affine space and elementary representation consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is basic semialgebraic if \[S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_i(x)\mathrel{\triangleright_i}0,\ i=1,\ldots,t\},\] where \(f_i\in\mathbb R[x]\) and \(\triangleright_i\in\{\geq,>,=,\neq\}\). It is basic closed semialgebraic if it has the form \[S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_1(x)\geq0,\ldots,f_t(x)\geq0\}.\] Every basic semialgebraic set can be expressed using polynomial inequalities \(f\geq0\) and a single disequality \(g\neq0\), and every real algebraic variety is basic closed semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic semialgebraic set is described by finitely many polynomial weak inequalities, strict inequalities, equalities, or disequalities. A basic closed semialgebraic set uses only weak inequalities. Every basic semialgebraic set can be rewritten using weak inequalities and one disequality, and every real algebraic variety is basic closed semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\{x:f_i(x)\mathrel{\triangleright_i}0\},\ \triangleright_i\in\{\geq,>,=,\neq\};\quad S\text{ basic closed}\iff S=\{x:f_i(x)\geq0\ \forall i\}

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Closed Semialgebraic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization over one conjunction of finitely many non-strict polynomial inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\) and \(r\geq0\) be integers, and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). A basic closed semialgebraic set is a set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) admitting a presentation \[K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,r\}.\] When \(r=0\), the conjunction is vacuous and \(K=\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the corresponding optimization model has value \[f^*:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x).\] A polynomial equality may be encoded by a pair of opposite non-strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic closed model minimizes a polynomial over one finite conjunction of non-strict polynomial inequalities; an empty conjunction gives the whole decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0\text{ for all }i=1,\ldots,r\}\) and \(f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Sets, Boundary Regularity, Corners, and Irredundant Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines boundary terminology for the basic closed components of a finite-union semialgebraic presentation. The malformed standalone phrase concerning a polynomial being 'at' a point is omitted rather than reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
S=\bigcup_{k=1}^mT_k,\qquad T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_1^k(x)\geq0,\ldots,g_{m_k}^k(x)\geq0\}.
\]
For $u\in\partial T_k$, define
\[
I_k(u)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m_k\}:g_i^k(u)=0\},
\]
which is nonempty. The point $u$ is nonsingular for $\partial T_k$ if $|I_k(u)|=1$ and the unique active polynomial satisfies $\nabla g_i^k(u)\neq0$; otherwise $u$ is singular. It is a corner point of $T_k$ if $|I_k(u)|>1$. For $u\in\partial S$ and $i\in I_k(u)$, $g_i^k$ is irredundant at $u$ relative to $\partial S$ if there is a sequence of nonsingular points $u_N\in V(g_i^k)\cap\partial S$ of $\partial T_k$ such that $u_N\to u$; otherwise it is redundant at $u$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary point of a basic closed component, the active set consists of the defining inequalities that vanish. A point is nonsingular when exactly one inequality is active and its gradient is nonzero, and it is a corner when multiple inequalities are active. An active inequality is irredundant relative to the union's boundary when nonsingular boundary points on its zero set approach the point.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Union Semialgebraic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive presentation by finitely many basic closed semialgebraic components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1,\ldots,K_s\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be basic closed semialgebraic sets with \(K_\ell=\{x:g_{\ell i}(x)\geq0, i=1,\ldots,r_\ell\}\). A finite-union model has feasible set \[K=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{s}K_\ell.\] For any polynomial \(f\), its optimal value decomposes as \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=\min_{1\leq\ell\leq s}\inf_{x\in K_\ell}f(x),\] using extended-real infima and assuming \(s\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-union model uses finitely many basic closed components; its infimum is the smallest componentwise infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\cup_{\ell=1}^sK_\ell}f(x)=\min_{1\leq\ell\leq s}\inf_{x\in K_\ell}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonic-difference representation of polynomial programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the increasing and difference-of-increasing definitions, closure under finite extrema, constraint aggregation, and auxiliary-variable objective reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f is increasing on [a,b] if a\le x'\le x\le b implies f(x')\le f(x), and is difference-of-increasing (d.m.) there if f=f_1-f_2 with f_1,f_2 increasing. Every polynomial is d.m. on \mathbb R_+^n by separating its positive- and negative-coefficient monomials, and finite pointwise minima and maxima of d.m. functions are d.m. Thus polynomial constraints f_j(x)\ge0 can be combined as g(x):=\min_j f_j(x)\ge0. If f_0=f_{01}-f_{02}, with f_{01},f_{02} increasing polynomials, introduce t with 0\le t\le f_{02}(b)-f_{02}(a) and impose f_{02}(x)+t-f_{02}(b)\ge0; the objective becomes f_{01}(x)+t-f_{02}(b). Consequently, after a possible lifting, the polynomial program can be written as \min\{f(x):g(x)\ge0,\ x\in[a,b]\}, where f is an increasing polynomial and g(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}\{u_j(x)-v_j(x)\} with u_j,v_j increasing polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing functions preserve componentwise order on a box, while difference-of-increasing functions are differences of two such functions. Every polynomial on the nonnegative orthant has this form, and finite minima and maxima preserve it. Polynomial constraints can therefore be aggregated into one minimum constraint, and an auxiliary variable can convert the objective so that any box-constrained polynomial program has an increasing polynomial objective and a constraint equal to a minimum of differences of increasing polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (P)\equiv\min\{f(x):g(x)\ge0,\ x\in[a,b]\},\qquad g(x)=\min_j\{u_j(x)-v_j(x)\},

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence, finite exactness, and extraction for rational moment–SOS relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of relaxations (10.3) and (10.4) in the referenced rational-minimization setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbf K\) be as in (5.2), let Assumption 2.14 hold, and consider the semidefinite relaxations (10.3) and (10.4). Then:

(a) \(\rho^*\) is finite and
\[
\rho_d^*\uparrow\rho^*,\qquad \rho_d\uparrow\rho^*\quad\text{as }d\to\infty.
\]

(b) If additionally \(\operatorname{int}(\mathbf K)\neq\varnothing\), then \(\rho_d^*=\rho_d\) for every \(d\).

(c) Let \(\mathbf x^*\in\mathbf K\) be a global minimizer of \(p/q\). If the polynomial \(p-\rho^*q\), which is nonnegative on \(\mathbf K\), has Putinar's representation (2.10), then problems (10.3) and (10.4) have optimal solutions, and for some \(d_0\in\mathbb N\),
\[
\rho_d^*=\rho_d=\rho^*\qquad\forall d\ge d_0.
\]

(d) If an optimal solution \(\mathbf y^*\) of (10.3) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_{d-v}(\mathbf y^*)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_d(\mathbf y^*)=s,
\qquad v=\max_j v_j,
\]
then there are \(s\) global minimizers, and they can be extracted by Algorithm 6.9.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced assumptions, both relaxation-value sequences increase to the finite rational optimum. If K has nonempty interior, their values agree at every order. If the optimality-gap polynomial has the stated Putinar representation, the relaxation problems attain optimal solutions and become exact from some finite order onward. An optimal moment solution satisfying the stated flat-rank condition yields s extractable global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf x^*\in\mathbf K\text{ is a global minimizer and }p-\rho^*q\text{ has Putinar's representation (2.10) for clause (c)}
\mathbf y^*\text{ is optimal for (10.3) and }\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_{d-v}(\mathbf y^*)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_d(\mathbf y^*)=s\text{ for clause (d)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_d^*\uparrow\rho^*,\quad\rho_d\uparrow\rho^*,\quad\text{together with clauses (b)--(d) under their respective additional hypotheses}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence and Flat-Rank Recovery for the Rational-Sum Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the semidefinite hierarchy (10.8); Assumption 2.14, \(v\), and the moment sequences retain their source definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Assumption 2.14 holds for the polynomials \((g_j)\) defining \(\mathbf K\). For the semidefinite relaxations (10.8), \(f_d^*\uparrow f^*\) as \(d\to\infty\). Moreover, let \((\mathbf y_i^d)_{i=1}^s\) be optimal and satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}M_d(\mathbf y_i^d)=\operatorname{rank}M_{d-v}(\mathbf y_i^d)=R\) for every \(i\). If \(R>1\), each corresponding truncated moment sequence has a representing measure supported on \(R\) points \(\mathbf x^\ell(i)\in\mathbf K\). If additionally \(\mathbf x^\ell(i)=\mathbf x^\ell(j)\) for all \(i\ne j\) and every \(\ell\), then \(f_d^*=f^*\), and all those points are global minimizers of \(\mathbf P\). If \(R=1\), then \(f_d^*=f^*\) and \(\mathbf x(i)=\mathbf x^*\) for every \(i\), where \(\mathbf x^*\in\mathbf K\) is a global minimizer of \(\mathbf P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Assumption 2.14, the SDP bounds increase to the global optimum. A common flat-rank condition gives finitely atomic representing measures; aligned atoms yield finite exactness and global minimizers, while rank one yields a common global minimizer and finite exactness.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Unions of Intervals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate polynomial minimization over finitely many nondegenerate compact interval components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\), and let \(K=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}[a_j,b_j]\), where \(m\ge 1\) and \(a_j<b_j<a_{j+1}\) for \(j<m\). Polynomial optimization over a finite union of intervals is the problem \[p^*=\min\{p(x):x\in K\}=\min_{1\le j\le m}\min_{x\in[a_j,b_j]}p(x).\] Compactness of \(K\) ensures that every component minimum and the global minimum are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a polynomial over finitely many disjoint nondegenerate compact intervals reduces to taking the smallest attained componentwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\min_{1\le j\le m}\min_{x\in[a_j,b_j]}p(x)\), and a minimizer exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected-Component Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise characterization of local and global minima on disconnected feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}K_j\subset\mathbb R\), where the nonempty compact sets \(K_j\) are pairwise disjoint and have positive mutual distance, and let \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\). Then \[\min_{x\in K}p(x)=\min_{1\le j\le m}\min_{x\in K_j}p(x).\] Moreover, any point minimizing \(p\) on one component \(K_j\) is a local minimizer relative to \(K\), but it is globally minimizing on \(K\) only when its value equals the smallest component minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated components create relative local minima componentwise, while global optimality requires comparing the minimum values across every component.
assumptions_latex: \(K_1,\ldots,K_m\) are nonempty compact sets with positive pairwise distance
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global minimization is componentwise comparison; a component minimizer need not minimize over all of \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linearly constrained quadratic programs and their curvature boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the model, its symmetric-matrix representation, and the consequences of positive-semidefinite versus indefinite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linearly constrained quadratic program can be written as \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\;Q(x)=c^Tx+\tfrac12x^TDx\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ax\le b,\;x\ge0.\] Because \(x^TDx=x^T((D+D^T)/2)x\), the matrix \(D\) may be assumed symmetric without changing the objective. Unrestricted variables may be replaced by differences of nonnegative variables. If \(D\succeq0\), the program is convex and every local minimizer is global; for finitely encoded rational data, convex quadratic programming admits polynomial-time algorithms. If \(D\not\succeq0\), the quadratic objective is nonconvex in general, and a local optimization procedure does not generally guarantee identification of a global optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly constrained quadratic program minimizes a quadratic objective subject to linear inequalities and nonnegative variables. The quadratic matrix can be symmetrized without changing the objective, and unrestricted variables can be represented using nonnegative variables. A positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix yields a convex problem, for which local minimizers are global and polynomial-time algorithms exist under finite rational encoding. Without positive semidefiniteness, the problem is generally nonconvex and local optimization has no general global-optimality guarantee.
assumptions_latex: c\in\mathbb R^n,\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}
\text{The polynomial-time claim assumes finitely encoded rational input data.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\succeq0\Rightarrow Q\text{ is convex and every local minimizer is global};\qquad D\not\succeq0\Rightarrow\text{no general global-optimality guarantee follows from local optimization alone.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: RLT relaxation-point branching rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies bounding, corner termination, and selection of the branching coordinate and split point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), solve \(LR(P_{M_k})\) on \(M_k=[p^k,q^k]\) and let \((x^k,y^k)\) be optimal, giving \(\beta(M_k)=l_0(x^k)+\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_{0\alpha}y_\alpha^k\). If \(x^k\) is a corner of \(M_k\), it is feasible for the original problem. Otherwise choose \(i_k\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le n}\eta_i^k\), where \(\eta_i^k=\min\{x_i^k-p_i^k,q_i^k-x_i^k\}\), and bisect \(M_k\) through \(x_{i_k}^k\) along coordinate \(i_k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical unconstrained quadratic minimization and its finite-optimum criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), a vector \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), an unconstrained quadratic model is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q(x),\qquad q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha.\] Its infimum is finite exactly when \(Q\succeq0\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q)\). Under these conditions, the minimizers are precisely the solutions of \(Qx=-c\); otherwise the infimum is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained quadratic has a finite minimum exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite and its linear term lies in the Hessian range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf q> -\infty\) iff \(Q\succeq0\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q)\); then \(\operatorname*{argmin}q=\{x:Qx=-c\}\).

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical QCQP with a quadratic objective and finitely many quadratic inequality or equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). A quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i(x)\le0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\qquad e_j(x)=0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,r,\] where \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i\) and \(e_j(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}R_jx+d_j^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_j\), with \(Q_i,R_j\in\mathbb S^n\). A standard convex QCQP subclass is obtained when \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and every equality function \(e_j\) is affine, equivalently \(R_j=0\). Outside such conditions, a QCQP may be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP optimizes a quadratic objective subject to finitely many quadratic inequalities and equalities. Positive-semidefinite objective and inequality Hessians together with affine equalities define the standard convex subclass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed model is a QCQP; \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and \(R_j=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,r\) define its standard convex subclass.

notation.meaning: symmetric Hessian matrices of the corresponding quadratic functions

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Problem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean-ball trust-region subproblems and generalized one-quadratic-constraint variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\), the classical trust-region subproblem is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad \lVert x\rVert_2\le\Delta.\] The matrix \(Q\) may be indefinite. A generalized trust-region model replaces the ball constraint by \(x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\le0\), where \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). The classical feasible ball is nonempty and compact, so its continuous quadratic objective attains a global minimum. This compactness conclusion does not automatically extend to the generalized constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical trust-region problem minimizes a possibly indefinite quadratic over a Euclidean ball and always attains its minimum. A generalized variant uses one quadratic inequality, whose feasible set need not be compact.
assumptions_latex: For the generalized variant, \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The classical trust-region problem has an attained global minimizer even when \(Q\) is indefinite.

notation.meaning: coefficients of the generalized quadratic constraint

knowledge_statements.title: Standard Quadratic Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic optimization over the standard simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard quadratic optimization problem associated with \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) is \[p^*=\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx:x\in\Delta_n\},\qquad \Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x=1\}.\] Because \(\Delta_n\) is nonempty and compact, the minimum is attained. The model is generally nonconvex when \(Q\) is not positive semidefinite on the affine hull of the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard quadratic optimization minimizes a quadratic form over the standard simplex; compactness guarantees attainment even when the objective is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=\min_{x\in\Delta_n}x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) exists and is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SOS-multiplier characterization of polynomial convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of global polynomial convexity through the midpoint-convexity polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}] is convex if and only if there exist nontrivial sum-of-squares polynomials p,q\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}] such that, for all \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\left(f(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{y})-2f\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}}{2}\right)\right)=q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is convex exactly when there are nontrivial sum-of-squares polynomials p and q such that multiplying its midpoint-convexity difference by p yields q identically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff \exists\text{ nontrivial }p,q\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}]\ \forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\left(f(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{y})-2f\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}}{2}\right)\right)=q(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Polynomial-Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex polynomial minimization over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be convex on \(C\). A convex polynomial-objective model is \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\] Every local minimizer is global, and the minimizer set is convex. If \(C\) is compact, the infimum is attained; more generally, attainment follows when \(C\) is closed and \(f\) is coercive on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex polynomial-objective model minimizes a convex polynomial on a convex set; local minima are global, with attainment under compactness or coercivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every local minimizer is global, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS-Convex Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial models whose objective and inequality-function Hessians admit sum-of-squares matrix factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is SOS-convex if there exists a polynomial matrix \(H(x)\) such that \[\nabla^2f(x)=H(x)^{\mathsf T}H(x).\] Under the inequality convention \(g_i(x)\le0\), an SOS-convex polynomial model minimizes an SOS-convex polynomial \(f_0\) subject to SOS-convex polynomial inequalities \(g_i(x)\le0\). The Hessian factorization gives \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), so every SOS-convex polynomial is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS-convexity means that a polynomial Hessian has a polynomial matrix Gram factorization. SOS-convex objectives and less-than-or-equal constraint functions therefore define a convex polynomial model.
assumptions_latex: There exists a polynomial matrix \(H(x)\) satisfying \(\nabla^2f(x)=H(x)^{\mathsf T}H(x)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), hence \(f\) is convex.

notation.meaning: SOS-convex polynomial inequality function under the convention g_i less than or equal to zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SOS matrix polynomials and SOS-convex polynomial descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines SOS-certifiable polynomial curvature and makes explicit that SOS-convexity of a basic set is relative to its displayed defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric matrix polynomial P\in\mathbb{R}[x]^{r\times r} is SOS if there exists a matrix polynomial W such that P(x)=W(x)^TW(x). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix polynomial is SOS when it factors as a polynomial matrix transpose times itself. A polynomial is SOS-convex when its Hessian has this property and SOS-concave when its negative is SOS-convex. A displayed basic semialgebraic description is SOS-convex when all its defining inequality polynomials are SOS-concave.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes SOS-convexity through the Hessian, midpoint gap, and first-order remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real polynomial \(g\), the following are equivalent: (a) \(g\) is SOS-convex; (b) \(\nabla^2g(\mathbf{x})\) is an SOS matrix polynomial; (c) \(\frac12g(\mathbf{x})+\frac12g(\mathbf{y})-g\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}}2\right)\) is SOS in \((\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\); and (d) \(g(\mathbf{x})-g(\mathbf{y})-\nabla g(\mathbf{y})^T(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\) is SOS in \((\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SDP lifts under SOS-convexity or strict quasiconcavity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient curvature conditions for exact moment semidefinite representations of compact convex basic semialgebraic sets, subject to Assumption 2.14.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\geq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be convex and compact with nonempty interior, and suppose Assumption 2.14 holds. If for every \(j\), either \(-g_j\) is SOS-convex or \(g_j\) is strictly quasiconcave on \(K\), then there exists \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that \[K=\left\{z:\exists y\in\mathbb R^{s(2d)},\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ M_{d-v_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\ \forall j,\ L_y(1)=1,\ L_y(x_i)=z_i\ \forall i\right\}.\] Hence \(K\) is semidefinite representable. If \(-g_j\) is SOS-convex for every \(j\), then for every \(d\geq\max_jv_j\), \[K=\left\{z:\exists y\in\mathbb R^{s(2d)},\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ L_y(g_j)\geq0\ \forall j,\ L_y(1)=1,\ L_y(x_i)=z_i\ \forall i\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Assumption 2.14, a compact convex basic semialgebraic set with nonempty interior has an exact moment SDP lift when every defining polynomial satisfies the stated SOS-convexity or strict-quasiconcavity condition. In the all-SOS-convex case, scalar moment inequalities replace localizing-matrix constraints.

\forall j,\ [-g_j\text{ is SOS-convex}]\lor[g_j\text{ is strictly quasiconcave on }K]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ has the stated exact moment-matrix SDP representation and hence is SDr}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) satisfy Slater's condition, and let \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)>-\infty\). If \(f\) and every \(-g_j\) are SOS-convex, then, at the source-defined order \(d\), \(f^*=\rho_d=\rho_d^*\). Moreover, if \(y\) is an optimal solution of the moment relaxation, then \(x^*:=(L_y(x_1),\ldots,L_y(x_n))\in K\) and \(f(x^*)=f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Slater's condition, the stated SOS and moment relaxations exactly solve an SOS-convex polynomial program. The first moments of any optimal moment solution form a feasible global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ satisfies Slater's condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*=\rho_d=\rho_d^*,\qquad y\text{ optimal}\Longrightarrow x^*:=(L_y(x_1),\ldots,L_y(x_n))\in K\text{ and }f(x^*)=f^*.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Semialgebraic-Set Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial optimization on convex feasible sets described by finitely many polynomial inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex basic semialgebraic feasible set is a set \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,r\}\] that is convex, where all \(g_i\) and \(h_j\) are real polynomials. A sufficient representation condition is that every \(g_i\) is convex and every \(h_j\) is affine. A convex semialgebraic-set model minimizes a convex polynomial over such a nonempty set \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These models minimize a convex polynomial over a convex set described by polynomial inequalities and equalities; convex inequalities and affine equalities suffice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing a convex polynomial over \(K\) is a convex polynomial optimization model.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Optimization Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization models whose cross-block interaction is bilinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty feasible sets. A bilinear optimization model has objective \[\inf_{x\in X,\ y\in Y}\ x^{\mathsf T}Ay+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha,\] possibly together with constraints that are affine in \(x\) for each fixed \(y\) and affine in \(y\) for each fixed \(x\). The model is separately affine in its two variable blocks but is generally nonconvex jointly because of the products \(x_i y_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bilinear models are affine in either variable block when the other is fixed, but their cross-products generally destroy joint convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is affine in each block separately and generally nonconvex in \((x,y)\) jointly.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Box-Constrained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional multilinear polynomial optimization over a Cartesian box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(\ell_i<u_i\). A multilinear box-constrained model has the form \[\min_{x\in B} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}c_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\] possibly with constraints \(g_j(x)\leq 0\), where every \(g_j\) has the same multilinear form. Equivalently, each participating polynomial is affine in every coordinate when all other coordinates are fixed. Because such a polynomial is coordinatewise affine, its unrestricted minimum and maximum over \(B\) are attained at vertices of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-constrained multilinear model optimizes polynomials that are affine in each coordinate separately; without additional constraints, extrema occur at box vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and any constraint polynomials are multilinear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the unconstrained model, \(\min_{x\in B}f(x)=\min_{x\in\operatorname{vert}(B)}f(x)\) and analogously for the maximum.

notation.meaning: coefficient of the square-free monomial indexed by S

knowledge_statements.title: Multiaffine Network Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorized multiaffine optimization on a network of variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite hypergraph and let each vertex \(v\) carry a block \(x_v\in B_v\subset\mathbb R^{n_v}\). A multiaffine network model is \[\min_{x\in\prod_{v\in V}B_v}\sum_{e\in E}\phi_e((x_v)_{v\in e})\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{e\in E}\psi_{je}((x_v)_{v\in e})\leq0,\] where every local factor \(\phi_e\) and \(\psi_{je}\) is affine in each incident block separately when the remaining blocks are fixed. The hypergraph records the interaction locality; it does not require joint affinity or convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables occupy network nodes, while objective and constraint factors couple only incident blocks and are affine in each block separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is a network-structured multiaffine polynomial optimization problem over \(\prod_{v\in V}B_v\).

knowledge_statements.title: Even-Degree Form Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization of real homogeneous forms of even degree on normalized or compact sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=2k\) and let \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a homogeneous form of degree \(d\), represented by a symmetric order-\(d\) tensor \(\mathcal A\) through \(p(x)=\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes d}\rangle\). Even-degree form optimization seeks \[p_{\min}=\min_{x\in K}p(x)\quad\text{or}\quad p_{\max}=\max_{x\in K}p(x),\] where \(K\) is commonly the unit sphere or another compact basic semialgebraic set. Since \(p(-x)=p(x)\), antipodal points have equal objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even-degree form model optimizes a homogeneous polynomial on a normalized compact domain; its value is unchanged by reversing the sign of the variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both extrema exist, and \(p(-x)=p(x)\) whenever \(x,-x\in K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Degree Form Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antipodal structure of odd-degree homogeneous optimization on centrally symmetric domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=2k+1\) and let \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be homogeneous of degree \(d\). If \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and centrally symmetric, then \(p(-x)=-p(x)\) for every \(x\in K\). Consequently, \[\min_{x\in K}p(x)=-\max_{x\in K}p(x).\] In particular, optimizing an odd-degree form over the unit sphere reduces either extremum to the other, and every nonzero odd-degree form takes both positive and negative values there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a centrally symmetric compact set, an odd-degree form changes sign at antipodal points, so its minimum is the negative of its maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in K}p(x)=-\max_{x\in K}p(x)\).

notation.meaning: central symmetry of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Eigenvalue Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real Z-eigenvalue formulation for symmetric tensors and sphere-constrained forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\in\operatorname{Sym}^m(\mathbb R^n)\). A real Z-eigenpair is a scalar-vector pair \((\lambda,x)\) satisfying \[\mathcal A x^{m-1}=\lambda x,\qquad x^\mathsf T x=1.\] For the homogeneous form \(f(x)=\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\rangle\), every first-order stationary point of its restriction to the unit sphere yields such a pair, with \(\lambda=f(x)\). Conversely, every Z-eigenpair is stationary for the sphere-constrained form problem. Thus extremal Z-eigenvalues are obtained by minimizing or maximizing \(f\) on the unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Z-eigenpairs of a real symmetric tensor are exactly stationary points of its homogeneous form on the Euclidean unit sphere.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a real symmetric tensor of order \(m\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A x^{m-1}=\lambda x\) holds exactly at sphere-stationary points, with \(\lambda=\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\rangle\).

notation.meaning: contraction of A with m−1 copies of x

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Singular-Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilinear singular values for real rectangular tensors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_m}\) and define \(F(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=\langle\mathcal A,x^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x^{(m)}\rangle\). A singular tuple consists of unit vectors \(x^{(k)}\in\mathbb R^{n_k}\) and a scalar \(\sigma\) such that, for every \(k\), \[\mathcal A\times_{j\ne k}x^{(j)}=\sigma x^{(k)},\qquad \|x^{(k)}\|_2=1.\] These equations are the first-order stationarity conditions for optimizing \(F\) over the product of unit spheres, and \(\sigma=F(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tensor singular tuples are stationary points of a rectangular tensor’s multilinear form over a product of Euclidean unit spheres.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a finite-dimensional real order-\(m\) tensor.
Every factor vector has Euclidean norm one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each stationary tuple satisfies \(\mathcal A\times_{j\ne k}x^{(j)}=\sigma x^{(k)}\) for all \(k\).

notation.meaning: contraction in every mode except k

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Tensor Spectral Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric spectral norm and its diagonal homogeneous-form reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real symmetric order-\(m\) tensor \(\mathcal A\in\operatorname{Sym}^m(\mathbb R^n)\), define its multilinear spectral norm over independent unit vectors. The symmetric spectral regime satisfies \[\max_{\|x^{(1)}\|_2=\cdots=\|x^{(m)}\|_2=1}\left|\left\langle\mathcal A,x^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x^{(m)}\right\rangle\right|=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\left|\left\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\right\rangle\right|.\] Hence a best rank-one spectral approximation may be chosen symmetric, and spectral optimization reduces to a homogeneous polynomial problem on one sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real symmetric tensor, the spectral norm can be computed using one repeated unit vector rather than independent mode vectors.
assumptions_latex: All norms on factor vectors are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\mathcal A\|_\sigma=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}|\langle\mathcal A,x^{\otimes m}\rangle|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Tensor Spectral Regimes

At any maximizing tuple, signs may be chosen so that the contraction is nonnegative, and the associated first-order equations are \(\mathcal A\times_{j\ne k}x^{(j)}=\|\mathcal A\|_\sigma x^{(k)}\) for every mode \(k\). Unlike the symmetric regime, the factors inhabit distinct mode spaces and need not coincide.

Each mode uses the Euclidean unit sphere.

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Norm Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization models regularized or constrained by finite-dimensional tensor norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb T=igotimes_{k=1}^m\mathbb R^{n_k}\) and let \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb T}\) be a tensor norm. A tensor norm model optimizes an objective \(F:\mathbb T\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) either as \[\min_{X\in\mathbb T}F(X)+\lambda\|X\|_{\mathbb T}\] or as \(\min F(X)\) subject to \(\|X\|_{\mathbb T}\leq\tau\), where \(\lambda,
\tau>0\). Common choices include the Frobenius, spectral, and nuclear norms; the selected norm determines geometry, computational difficulty, and the structural bias imposed on \(X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Rank Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical polyadic rank and rank-constrained tensor optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\inigotimes_{k=1}^m\mathbb R^{n_k}\), its canonical polyadic rank is \[\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)=\min\left\{r:X=
\sum_{i=1}^r u_i^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_i^{(m)}\right\},\] with \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(0)=0\). A tensor rank model minimizes a loss \(F(X)\) subject to \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)\leq r\), or penalizes the loss by \(\lambda\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)\). For \(m=2\) this is matrix rank; for \(m\geq3\), the feasible geometry can be nonclosed and substantially more singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CP rank is the fewest rank-one outer products representing a tensor; rank models constrain or penalize that number.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) belongs to a finite-dimensional real tensor-product space.
Rank-one terms are unrestricted outer products of mode vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)\) is the minimum number of rank-one tensor summands representing \(X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Based Rank Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tensor nuclear norm as a convex gauge surrogate for CP rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal U\) be the set of rank-one tensors \(u^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u^{(m)}\) with \(\|u^{(k)}\|_2=1\) for every \(k\). The tensor nuclear norm is the atomic gauge \[\|X\|_*=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r|\alpha_i|:X=\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha_iU_i,
\ U_i\in\mathcal U\right\}.\] It is convex and is dual to the tensor spectral norm: \[\|X\|_*=\max_{\|Y\|_\sigma\leq1}\langle X,Y\rangle.\] Replacing CP rank by \(\|X\|_*\) therefore gives a norm-based convex surrogate, though it need not preserve every rank minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tensor nuclear norm gauges normalized rank-one atoms, is dual to the spectral norm, and supplies a convex surrogate for CP rank.
assumptions_latex: The ambient tensor space is finite-dimensional and real.
Rank-one atoms have unit Euclidean norm in every mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|X\|_*\) is convex and satisfies \(\|X\|_*=\max_{\|Y\|_\sigma\leq1}\langle X,Y\rangle\).

notation.meaning: set of normalized rank-one tensor atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Stratified Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of tensor feasible regions by exact CP rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a subset of a finite-dimensional tensor space and define \(C_{\leq r}=\{X\in C:\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)\leq r\}\) and \(C_r=\{X\in C:\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CP}}(X)=r\}\). Then \[C_{\leq r}=\bigcup_{s=0}^r C_s,\qquad C_r=C_{\leq r}\setminus C_{\leq r-1}.\] These exact-rank pieces form the CP-rank stratification of \(C\). For tensors of order at least three, bounded-rank sets need not be closed, so limits of sequences in \(C_{\leq r}\) may have rank exceeding \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tensor feasible set decomposes into exact-CP-rank pieces; in higher order, bounded-rank sets may fail to be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) lies in a finite-dimensional real tensor space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\leq r}=\bigcup_{s=0}^rC_s\) and \(C_r=C_{\leq r}\setminus C_{\leq r-1}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constancy on the Face Determined by an Optimal Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property of maximizers of multilinear polynomials over the unit hypercube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=[0,1]^n\), let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be a multilinear polynomial, and let \(x^*\in U\) maximize \(f\) over \(U\). Define \(J=\{i:x_i^*\in\{0,1\}\}\) and \(U(x^*)=\{x\in U:x_i=x_i^*\text{ for every }i\in J\}\). Then \(f(x)=f(x^*)\) for every \(x\in U(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a multilinear polynomial maximized over the unit hypercube, fixing every coordinate that is integral at a maximizer defines a face on which the polynomial is everywhere equal to its maximum value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in U(x^*),\quad f(x)=f(x^*)

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Encodings of Combinatorial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies when a polynomial formulation exactly represents a finite combinatorial optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite feasible family with cost \(c:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R\). An exact polynomial encoding consists of a basic semialgebraic set \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ h_k(x)=0\}\] and a decoding map \(\phi:K\to\mathcal C\) such that \(\phi\) is bijective and \(f(x)=c(\phi(x))\) for every \(x\in K\). Under these conditions, \[\min_{u\in\mathcal C}c(u)=\min_{x\in K}f(x),\] and minimizers correspond through \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact polynomial encoding bijectively represents combinatorial feasible objects and preserves their costs, hence preserves optimal values and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{u\in\mathcal C}c(u)=\min_{x\in K}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: FPNulLA Solution-Counting Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative closure and dual-dimension stabilization procedure for counting solutions with multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $F\subset\mathbb K[x]$, initialize $d=\deg(F)$. Repeatedly return $0$ if $1\in F$; replace $F$ by $F^+\cap\mathbb K[x]_d$ until $F=F^+\cap\mathbb K[x]_d$, checking after each replacement whether $1\in F$; if $\dim_d(F^\circ)=\dim_{d-1}(F^\circ)$, return $\dim_d(F^\circ)$; otherwise set $F\leftarrow F^+$ and $d\leftarrow d+1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FPNulLA repeatedly closes the polynomial space under truncated prolongation. It returns zero if the certificate one is found; when the truncated-annihilator dimension stabilizes, it returns that dimension as the number of solutions over the field up to multiplicity; otherwise it increases the degree and continues.
assumptions_latex: F\subseteq\mathbb K[x]\text{ is a vector space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The returned value is the number of solutions of }F(x)=0\text{ over }\mathbb K\text{ up to multiplicities, with }0\text{ returned for infeasibility.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oriented-Cycle Parity Certificate for Non-3-Colorability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient certificate constructed from oriented partial 3-cycles and chordless 4-cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ have edge set $E$ and associated arc set $A$. If there exists a set $C$ of oriented partial $3$-cycles and oriented chordless $4$-cycles such that $|C_{(i,j)}|+|C_{(j,i)}|\equiv0\pmod 2$ for every $(i,j)\in E$ and $\sum_{(i,j)\in A,\,i<j}|C_{(i,j)}|\equiv1\pmod 2$, where $|C_{(i,j)}|$ is the number of cycles in $C$ containing arc $(i,j)$, then $G$ is not $3$-colorable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is not 3-colorable if it has a set of oriented partial triangles and oriented chordless four-cycles such that each edge has even total use across its two orientations, while the total use of arcs directed from the smaller to the larger endpoint is odd.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a set of oriented partial }3\text{-cycles and oriented chordless }4\text{-cycles}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is not }3\text{-colorable}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial encodings of stable sets, graph colorings, and cut-contained edge sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polynomial representations of three classical graph structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E). For k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}, the system x_i^2-x_i=0\ (i\in V),\ x_ix_j=0\ (\{i,j\}\in E),\ \sum_{i\in V}x_i=k is feasible if and only if G has a stable set of size k. The system x_i^k-1=0\ (i\in V),\ \sum_{s=0}^{k-1}x_i^{k-1-s}x_j^s=0\ (\{i,j\}\in E) has a complex solution if and only if G is k-colorable; when k is odd, the same equivalence holds over \overline{\mathbb F}_2. The incidence vectors of edge subsets contained in cuts are exactly the binary vectors satisfying x_e^2-x_e=0\ (e\in E) and \prod_{e\in T}x_e=0 for every odd cycle T. Consequently, for w_e\ge0, the maximum-weight member of this family has the max-cut value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable sets of a prescribed size, proper graph colorings, and edge subsets contained in cuts admit the stated exact polynomial encodings. The coloring characterization is over the complex numbers and, for odd k, over the algebraic closure of the two-element field. For nonnegative weights, optimization over the cut-contained edge sets has the max-cut value.
assumptions_latex: w_e\ge0\quad(e\in E)\text{ for the max-cut conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed systems characterize stable sets of size }k,\ k\text{-colorings, and cut-contained edge subsets, respectively.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-degree Nullstellensatz feasibility test for polynomial equations over a field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite-dimensional vector space $F\subseteq\mathbb K[x]$ and a Nullstellensatz bound $D$, for $k=0,1,\ldots,D$, return $\mathrm{INFEASIBLE}$ if $1\in F$ and otherwise replace $F$ by $F^+$. If no membership test succeeds, return $\mathrm{FEASIBLE}$.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns INFEASIBLE if }1\in F\text{ is detected and otherwise returns FEASIBLE after the bounded iterations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parallel-layer bound implies theta-body exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides a facetwise geometric sufficient condition for finite-level theta-body exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be finite and let \(t\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\). Suppose that for every facet \(F\) of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), there is a hyperplane \(H_F\) satisfying \(H_F\cap\operatorname{conv}(S)=F\), and that \(S\) is contained in at most \(t+1\) parallel translates of \(H_F\). Then \(I(S)\) is \(\operatorname{TH}_t\)-exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the points of a finite set occupy at most t+1 parallel layers relative to a supporting hyperplane for every facet of their convex hull, then their vanishing ideal is exact at theta-body level t.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is contained in at most }t+1\text{ parallel translates of each }H_F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(S)\text{ is }\operatorname{TH}_t\text{-exact}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Iteration Complexity of NulLA and FPNulLA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time bounds when the number of algorithm iterations is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $L\in\mathbb N$ and let $F=\operatorname{span}\{f_1,\ldots,f_m\}\subseteq\mathbb K[x]$ be finite dimensional, with polynomials encoded as coefficient vectors indexed by all monomials of degree at most $\deg(F)$. The first $L$ iterations of the NulLA for-loop are computable in time polynomial in $n$ and the input size of the defining basis of $F$. If $\mathbb K$ is finite, the first $L$ iterations of the FPNulLA outer loop are computable in time polynomial in $n$, $\log_2|\mathbb K|$, and that basis-input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed L, the first L NulLA for-loop iterations take polynomial time in the number of variables and the encoded basis size. Over a finite field, the first L outer FPNulLA iterations take polynomial time also in the binary logarithm of the field size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis-Independent Multivariate SOS Gram Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite Gram characterization expressed using arbitrary polynomial and dual-space bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x]_{n,2d}\). Choose bases \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_s\}\) of \(\mathbb{R}[x]_{n,d}\) and \(\{w_1,\ldots,w_t\}\) of \(\mathbb{R}[x]_{n,2d}^{*}\), where \(s=\binom{n+d}{d}\) and \(t=\binom{n+2d}{2d}\). Then \(p\) is a sum of squares if and only if there exists \(Q\in\mathcal{S}^{s}\) with \(Q\succeq0\) such that \(\langle p,w_k\rangle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{s}Q_{ij}\langle v_iv_j,w_k\rangle\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arbitrary bases of the degree-d polynomial space and the dual of the degree-2d polynomial space, a polynomial is SOS exactly when a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix satisfies all corresponding affine coefficient constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is SOS}\iff\exists Q\in\mathcal{S}^{s},\ Q\succeq0:\ \langle p,w_k\rangle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{s}Q_{ij}\langle v_iv_j,w_k\rangle\ \forall k=1,\ldots,t.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Rank Point of a Free Polynomial Variety
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surjectivity-based regularity condition and its dimensional consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \((X,v)\in\mathcal V_n(p)\) is full rank if the linear map \(L_{X,v}:(\mathbb S^{n\times n})^g\to\mathbb R^n\), \(L_{X,v}(H)=p'(X)[H]v\), is surjective. Since \(\dim(\mathbb S^{n\times n})^g=g(n^2+n)/2\), one has \(\operatorname{codim}\ker L_{X,v}\le n\), with equality if and only if \((X,v)\) is full rank; in that case \(\operatorname{codim}\mathcal T_p(X,v)=n\). For \(n=1\), full rank is equivalent to \(\nabla\check p(X)\ne0\), so \(X\) is a nonsingular point of the commutative zero variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is full rank when the derivative map from symmetric matrix directions onto the vector space is surjective. Its kernel has codimension at most n, attaining n exactly at full-rank points; hence the clamped tangent plane then has codimension n. At scalar size this is the usual nonvanishing-gradient condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (X,v)\text{ is full rank}\iff L_{X,v}\text{ is onto}\iff\operatorname{codim}\mathcal T_p(X,v)=n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Curvature Forces Degree at Most Two
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rigidity theorem for symmetric noncommutative defining polynomials on their full-rank locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a symmetric noncommutative polynomial in \(g\) symmetric variables, let \(\mathcal O\) be a noncommutative basic open semialgebraic set, and let \(\mathcal R\) be the full-rank points of \(p\) in \(\mathcal V(p)\cap\mathcal O\). If \(\mathcal R\ne\varnothing\), \(\mathcal V(p)\) has positive curvature at every point of \(\mathcal R\), and \(p\) is a minimum-degree defining polynomial for \(\mathcal R\), then \(\deg p\le2\) and \(p\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the full-rank locus of a symmetric noncommutative polynomial is nonempty, has nonnegative clamped curvature everywhere, and is defined by p with minimum possible degree, then p has degree at most two and is concave.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal O\text{ is a noncommutative basic open semialgebraic set}
\mathcal R=\{(X,v)\in\mathcal V(p)\cap\mathcal O:(X,v)\text{ is full rank}\}\ne\varnothing
p\text{ is a minimum-degree defining polynomial for }\mathcal R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \deg(p)\le2\quad\text{and}\quad p\text{ is concave}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PSD middle matrices have truncated block support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard middle-matrix representation and its degree parameter \(\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)[h]\) be a symmetric noncommutative polynomial homogeneous of degree two in \(h\), with middle matrix \(Z=(Z_{ij})\) in the canonical block form (8.21). q(x)[h]\text{ is homogeneous of degree }2\text{ in }h

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Free Variety, Clamped Tangent Plane, and Clamped Second Fundamental Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a noncommutative polynomial evaluated on tuples of real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb{R}\langle x\rangle\), define \(\mathcal V(p)=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\mathcal V_n(p)\), where \(\mathcal V_n(p)=\{(X,v)\in(\mathbb S^{n\times n})^g\times\mathbb R^n:p(X)v=0\}\). At \((X,v)\in\mathcal V_n(p)\), the clamped tangent plane is \(\mathcal T_p(X,v)=\{H\in(\mathbb S^{n\times n})^g:p'(X)[H]v=0\}\), and the clamped second fundamental form is \(H\mapsto-\langle p''(X)[H]v,v\rangle\) on \(\mathcal T_p(X,v)\). Moreover, \(\{X:\exists v\ne0,\ (X,v)\in\mathcal V_n(p)\}=\{X:\det p(X)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The free variety of p consists, over every matrix size, of pairs (X,v) for which p(X)v vanishes. Its clamped tangent directions annihilate v under the directional derivative of p, and its clamped second fundamental form is the negative Hessian quadratic form restricted to those directions. The projected singular locus is exactly the determinant-zero locus of p(X).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal T_p(X,v)=\ker\bigl(H\mapsto p'(X)[H]v\bigr),\qquad \mathrm{II}^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,X,v}(H)=-\langle p''(X)[H]v,v\rangle.
