knowledge_statements.statement_title: Middle-Matrix Positivity on the Full-Rank Locus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positivity-transfer theorem for polynomials quadratic in direction variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,\mathcal O,\mathcal R\) satisfy the setting and hypotheses of the positive-curvature degree-two theorem. Let \(q(x)[h]\) be quadratic in \(h\) and admit a middle-matrix representation \(q=V^{\top}ZV\) with \(\deg V\le\deg p\). If \(v^{\top}q(X)[H]v\ge0\) for every \((X,v)\in\mathcal R\) and every \(H\), then \(Z(X)\succeq0\) for every \(X\) occurring in a pair \((X,v)\in\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the full-rank, positive-curvature, and minimum-degree setting, pointwise positivity of a direction-quadratic noncommutative polynomial on the full-rank locus forces its middle matrix to be positive semidefinite at every matrix tuple represented in that locus, provided the border-vector degree does not exceed the degree of p.
assumptions_latex: p,\mathcal O,\mathcal R\text{ satisfy the hypotheses of the positive-curvature degree-two theorem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall X\text{ such that }\exists v\ ((X,v)\in\mathcal R),\quad Z(X)\succeq0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Degree Defining Polynomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree minimality among nonzero noncommutative polynomials vanishing on a prescribed subset of a free variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be symmetric and let \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal V(p)\). Then \(p\) is a minimum-degree defining polynomial for \(\mathcal D\) if, for every nonzero noncommutative polynomial \(q\), not necessarily symmetric, \([\forall(X,v)\in\mathcal D,\ q(X)v=0]\Rightarrow\deg q\ge\deg p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric polynomial p is a minimum-degree defining polynomial for a nonempty subset D of its free variety when every nonzero noncommutative polynomial vanishing on all pairs in D has degree at least that of p; competing polynomials need not be symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall(X,v)\in\mathcal D,\ q(X)v=0\bigr)\Longrightarrow\deg(q)\ge\deg(p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalarization of Polynomial-Matrix Positivity and SOS Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates a symmetric polynomial matrix to its associated quadratic-form polynomial in the original and auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(x)\in\mathbb R[x]^{m\times m}\) be symmetric for \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and define \(p(x,y)=y^TP(x)y\) for \(y\in\mathbb R^m\). Then \(P(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(p(x,y)\ge0\) for every \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+m}\). Moreover, \(P\) is an SOS matrix if and only if \(p\) is a sum of squares in \(\mathbb R[x,y]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise positive semidefiniteness of a symmetric polynomial matrix is equivalent to global nonnegativity of its quadratic-form scalarization, and the matrix is SOS exactly when the scalarization is SOS.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall x,\ P(x)\succeq0\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall x,y,\ p(x,y)\ge0\bigr),\qquad P\text{ is an SOS matrix}\iff p\in\Sigma[x,y].

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Matrix Inequality Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility and optimization models constrained by positive-semidefinite polynomial matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial matrix inequality model has decision vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), scalar polynomial objective \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\), and symmetric polynomial matrices \(F_1,\ldots,F_s\in\mathbb S^r[x]\). Its feasible set is \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:F_\ell(x)\succeq0\text{ for }\ell=1,\ldots,s\},\] and its optimization form is \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\). The condition \(F_\ell(x)\succeq0\) means \(v^{\mathsf T}F_\ell(x)v\ge0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial matrix inequality model optimizes a scalar polynomial over points where specified symmetric polynomial matrices are positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: All matrix entries and \(f\) are real polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\bigcap_{\ell=1}^s\{x:F_\ell(x)\succeq0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Valued Polynomial Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Loewner order to define minimization of a symmetric polynomial-matrix objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be feasible and let \(F\in\mathbb S^r[x]\). A matrix-valued polynomial objective model seeks Loewner-minimal values of \(F(x)\) over \(K\). A feasible point \(x^\star\in K\) is Loewner-minimal if no \(y\in K\) satisfies both \(F(y)\preceq F(x^\star)\) and \(F(y)\ne F(x^\star)\). For any weight \(W\succeq0\), scalarization produces the polynomial objective \(x\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(WF(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a symmetric polynomial matrix, and solutions are minimal under the positive-semidefinite order; positive-semidefinite trace weights yield scalar polynomial objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ is minimal}\iff\nexists y\in K:\ F(y)\preceq F(x^\star),\ F(y)\ne F(x^\star)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Loewner minimality is the canonical partial-order formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Loewner-minimality formulation and trace scalarization are mathematically plausible and the definition fits the terminal, but no inspectable citation is supplied. A source addressing matrix-valued optimization under the Loewner order is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Convex Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matrix convexity for symmetric polynomial-matrix mappings on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(F\in\mathbb S^r[x]\). The mapping \(F\) is matrix convex on \(C\) when, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preceq \theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y).\] A matrix-convex polynomial model minimizes \(F\) in the Loewner order, or a monotone scalarization of \(F\), over a convex feasible set; equivalently, every quadratic form \(x\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}F(x)v\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric polynomial matrix is matrix convex when it satisfies Jensen’s inequality in the Loewner order, equivalently after every quadratic-form scalarization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is matrix convex on }C\iff v^{\mathsf T}F(\cdot)v\text{ is convex on }C\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial and Unconstrained Polynomial Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial programs over real variables and the unconstrained subclass, allowing an unbounded-below objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A polynomial programming problem has the form
\[
\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{subject to}\quad p_j(\mathbf{x})=0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\qquad p_j(\mathbf{x})\ge 0\ (j=m+1,\ldots,m+s),
\]
where \(f,p_j\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]\). An unconstrained polynomial program is \(\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(\mathbf{x})\); its infimum \(f_*\) may equal \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial program minimizes a real multivariate polynomial subject to finitely many polynomial equalities and nonnegativity inequalities. Its unconstrained form minimizes a polynomial over all of real n-space, and its infimum may be minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_*:=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\quad\text{in the unconstrained case}.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Degree Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records total and coordinatewise degrees of a scalar polynomial objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonzero objective polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), its objective degree profile is \[D_{\mathrm{obj}}(f):=(d;\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n),\qquad d:=\deg f,\quad \delta_i:=\deg_{x_i}f.\] Here \(d\) is the largest total exponent among monomials with nonzero coefficient, while \(\delta_i\) is the largest exponent of \(x_i\). Consequently, \(\max_i\delta_i\le d\le\sum_i\delta_i\). For the zero polynomial, every degree component is assigned \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective degree profile records a polynomial’s total degree and its degree in each decision variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{obj}}(f)=(\deg f;\deg_{x_1}f,\ldots,\deg_{x_n}f)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure and recognition of odd-degree quasiconvex and pseudoconvex polynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ridge-polynomial characterization and fixed-degree polynomial-time recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}] have odd degree. It is quasiconvex only if and only if it has the form f(\mathbf{x})=h(\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{x}) for some nonzero \mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n and a monotone univariate polynomial h; the same representation characterizes pseudoconvexity, with the additional requirement that h' have no real root. Moreover, for every fixed odd degree d, quasiconvexity and pseudoconvexity of degree-d polynomials can each be decided in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd-degree quasiconvex polynomial depends on a single linear form through a monotone univariate polynomial. Odd-degree pseudoconvex polynomials have the same ridge form, additionally with a derivative having no real zero. For every fixed odd degree, both properties can be recognized in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\mathbf{x})=h(\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{x});\quad f\text{ pseudoconvex}\implies h'(t)\neq0\ \forall t\in\mathbb{R};\quad\text{for fixed odd }d,\text{ recognition is polynomial-time.}

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Mismatch Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies constrained models by the gap between objective and maximum constraint degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a polynomial optimization problem with nonzero objective \(f\) and nonzero constraints \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\). Let \(d_0:=\deg f\) and \(d_c:=\max_j\deg g_j\). Its degree-mismatch index is \(\Delta:=d_0-d_c\). The model is objective-dominant when \(\Delta>0\), degree-balanced when \(\Delta=0\), and constraint-dominant when \(\Delta<0\). The magnitude \(|\Delta|\) records the total-degree gap but does not by itself determine convexity, boundedness, or computational complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare the objective degree with the largest constraint degree: the model is objective-dominant, balanced, or constraint-dominant according to the sign of their difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta=\deg f-\max_j\deg g_j\).

knowledge_statements.title: Even-Degree Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a sufficient boundedness condition for unconstrained even-degree polynomial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) have even degree \(2r\ge2\), and let \(f_{2r}\) denote its leading homogeneous component. If \(f_{2r}(u)>0\) for every \(u\ne0\), then \(f\) is coercive: \[\|x\|\to\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)\to+\infty.\] Consequently, every sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is compact, and \(f\) attains a finite global minimum on \(\mathbb R^n\). Even degree alone is insufficient without a condition on the leading form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even-degree polynomial with a positive-definite leading form is coercive and attains a global minimum; even degree by itself does not ensure boundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is coercive and }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) be a nonconstant polynomial of odd degree \(d\). Then \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)=-\infty,\qquad \sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)=+\infty.\] This conclusion concerns the unconstrained domain \(\mathbb R^n\); constraints can exclude the directions along which the objective diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonconstant odd-degree real polynomial is unbounded above and below on the full space, although constraints can exclude its diverging directions.

children.title: Mixed-Parity Polynomial Regimes
children.top_down_role: Models combining even-degree and odd-degree polynomial components.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Parity Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies models whose objective-constraint degree vector contains both degree parities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constrained polynomial model with nonzero objective \(f\) and nonzero constraints \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\), define its degree-parity profile by \[P:=\bigl(\deg f\bmod 2,\deg g_1\bmod 2,\ldots,\deg g_m\bmod 2\bigr).\] The model lies in a mixed-parity regime exactly when \(P\) contains both \(0\) and \(1\); equivalently, at least one polynomial among \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) has even total degree and at least one has odd total degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model has mixed parity when the total degrees of its objective and constraints include at least one even degree and at least one odd degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\deg f\bmod2,\deg g_1\bmod2,\ldots,\deg g_m\bmod2\}=\{0,1\}\).

children.title: Parity-Dependent Boundedness
children.top_down_role: Boundedness behavior associated with polynomial degree parity.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Dependent Boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained real-domain boundedness; even degree is necessary, while a positive-definite leading form is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=p_d+p_{d-1}+\cdots+p_0\), where each \(p_k\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\) and \(p_d\ne0\). If \(d\) is odd, then \(p\) is unbounded both above and below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Consequently, a nonconstant polynomial that is bounded above or bounded below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) must have even degree. Even degree alone does not imply boundedness. If \(p_d(v)>0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), then \(p\) is coercive, bounded below, and attains a finite global minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant real polynomial bounded on either side must have even degree. Even degree alone is insufficient, while a positive-definite leading form guarantees coercivity and attainment of a finite global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(p_d\) is the degree-\(d\) homogeneous component of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(p\) is bounded above or below on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(d\) is even; if \(p_d(v)>0\) for every \(v\ne0\), then \(p\) is coercive and attains a finite global minimum.

notation.meaning: Leading homogeneous component of the polynomial.

children.title: Homogeneous Polynomial Structure
children.top_down_role: Models whose relevant polynomial components share ordinary scaling structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Polynomial Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary homogeneity of nonzero polynomials under uniform scalar dilation of all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_0^n}c_\alpha x^\alpha\) be nonzero with finite support. The polynomial \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(d\in\mathbb{N}_0\) if every \(\alpha\) with \(c_\alpha\ne0\) satisfies \(|\alpha|=d\). Equivalently, \(p(tx)=t^d p(x)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For nonzero \(p\), the degree \(d\) is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero polynomial is homogeneous of degree d when all supported monomials have total degree d, equivalently when uniform scaling multiplies its value by the d-th power.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(d\) exactly when \(p(tx)=t^d p(x)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Ordinary total degree of a multi-index.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of an ordinary homogeneous polynomial

children.title: Quasihomogeneous Polynomial Structure
children.top_down_role: Models whose polynomial components follow weighted scaling structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is \(w\)-quasihomogeneous of weighted degree \(D\) exactly when \(p(t^{w_1}x_1,\ldots,t^{w_n}x_n)=t^D p(x)\) for all \(t>0\).

notation.meaning: Weighted degree of a monomial exponent.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weighted-homogeneity definition with positive rational weights
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-weight polynomial quasihomogeneity; weights may be cleared to positive integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha\). The polynomial is quasihomogeneous with weight vector \(w\) and weighted degree \(D\) when every \(\alpha\) with \(c_\alpha\ne0\) satisfies \(w\cdot\alpha=D\). Equivalently, for the anisotropic dilation \(\delta_t(x)=(t^{w_1}x_1,\ldots,t^{w_n}x_n)\), one has \(p(\delta_t(x))=t^D p(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(t>0\). Multiplying \(w\) and \(D\) by a common positive number leaves the structure unchanged; rational weights can therefore be normalized to integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is quasihomogeneous when all its monomials share one positive weighted degree, equivalently when anisotropic coordinate scaling multiplies the polynomial by a fixed power.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasihomogeneous Polynomial Structure

children.title: Weighted-Degree Coordinate Structure
children.top_down_role: Coordinate organizations induced by variable-specific degree weights.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted coordinate degree is \(\deg_w(x^\alpha)=w\cdot\alpha\), and \(\deg_w(p)=\max_{\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)}w\cdot\alpha\) for \(p\ne0\).

notation.meaning: Positive weight assigned to coordinate i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weighted-degree grading of a polynomial ring
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate weights induce a grading or filtration on the polynomial ring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign coordinate \(x_i\) the positive weight \(w_i\). The weighted degree of the monomial \(x^\alpha\) is \(\deg_w(x^\alpha)=w\cdot\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\alpha_i\). For a nonzero polynomial \(p=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha\), define \(\deg_w(p)=\max\{w\cdot\alpha:c_\alpha\ne0\}\). Its weighted-degree-\(D\) component is the sum of those terms satisfying \(w\cdot\alpha=D\). Consequently, multiplication adds weighted degrees, while addition satisfies \(\deg_w(p+q)\le\max\{\deg_w(p),\deg_w(q)\}\) whenever \(p+q\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive coordinate weights assign each monomial the dot product of its exponent and weight vectors; a polynomial's weighted degree is the largest such value in its support.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Degree Coordinate Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-degree definition and stated algebraic properties are standard and internally consistent, but the record has no source or locator.

children.title: Scaling-Orbit Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-set and objective geometry associated with homogeneous scaling orbits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each orbit \(\mathcal{O}_w(x)=\{\delta_t(x):t>0\}\) satisfies \(p(\delta_t(x))=t^D p(x)\), so its intersection with \(\{p=0\}\) is either empty or the entire orbit.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct geometric consequence of weighted homogeneity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of positive anisotropic dilation orbits and invariant polynomial level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The maps \(\delta_t\) form an action of \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) because \(\delta_s(\delta_t(x))=\delta_{st}(x)\). Quasihomogeneity gives \(p(\delta_t(x))=t^D p(x)\) along every orbit. Hence the zero set \(Z(p)=\{x:p(x)=0\}\) is a union of scaling orbits. If \(D>0\) and \(p(x)\ne0\), the sign of \(p\) is constant on \(\mathcal{O}_w(x)\), and each positive level \(p=c\) on that orbit is reached at most once. For uniform weights this reduces to ordinary radial rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted dilations partition space into scaling orbits. A quasihomogeneous polynomial scales by one power along each orbit, making its zero set orbit-invariant and preserving sign.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Orbit Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit action, scaling law, zero-set invariance, and sign claim are correct under the stated positive-weight assumptions, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Multidegree Structure
children.top_down_role: Polynomial classes indexed by degree profiles across individual variables or variable groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidegree Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise multidegree for a polynomial in fixed variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(d_i=\max\{\alpha_i:\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)\}\). The coordinate multidegree is \(\operatorname{mdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\). Equivalently, \(d_i\) is the degree of \(p\) as a univariate polynomial in \(x_i\) over the polynomial ring in the remaining variables. Every \(\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)\) satisfies \(\alpha_i\le d_i\) for every \(i\), but \((d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) need not belong to \(\operatorname{supp}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multidegree records the largest exponent attained in each coordinate separately; these maxima need not occur together in any single monomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate multidegree of \(p\) is \(\operatorname{mdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\), where \(d_i=\max_{c_\alpha\ne0}\alpha_i\).

notation.meaning: Degree of p in coordinate variable i.

children.title: Block-Degree Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Degree Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total degree is measured separately within each fixed variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_m\), assign each exponent \(\alpha\) the block-degree vector \((|\alpha|_{B_1},\ldots,|\alpha|_{B_m})\), where \(|\alpha|_{B_j}=\sum_{i\in B_j}\alpha_i\). For nonzero \(p\), define \(\operatorname{bdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\), where \(d_j=\max_{\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)}|\alpha|_{B_j}\). Every supported monomial lies in \(\prod_{j=1}^m\{0,\ldots,d_j\}\), but the maximal corner need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After variables are partitioned into blocks, block degree records the largest total exponent appearing within each block, with maxima computed independently.
assumptions_latex: The variables are partitioned into nonempty disjoint blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block-degree vector is \(\operatorname{bdeg}(p)=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\), where \(d_j=\max_{c_\alpha\ne0}\sum_{i\in B_j}\alpha_i\).

children.title: Cross-Block Degree Coupling
children.top_down_role: Degree patterns created by monomials spanning multiple variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Degree Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based coupling among degree choices of distinct variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\alpha\in A\), define \(\gamma(\alpha)=(|\alpha|_{B_1},\ldots,|\alpha|_{B_m})\) and \(\Gamma(A)=\{\gamma(\alpha):\alpha\in A\}\). Let \(\Gamma_j(A)\) be the projection of \(\Gamma(A)\) onto coordinate \(j\). The support has no cross-block degree coupling when \(\Gamma(A)=\Gamma_1(A)\times\cdots\times\Gamma_m(A)\), and it has cross-block degree coupling when this equality fails. This predicate concerns jointly realized degree patterns, not coefficient factorization or functional separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block degrees are coupled when some combination of degrees observed separately in different blocks never occurs jointly in the polynomial's monomial support.
assumptions_latex: The variables are partitioned into nonempty disjoint blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-block degree coupling is present exactly when \(\Gamma(A)\ne\Gamma_1(A)\times\cdots\times\Gamma_m(A)\).

notation.meaning: Set of jointly realized block-degree vectors.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The monomial support of \(p\) is the finite set \(A=\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_0^n:c_\alpha\ne0\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monomials, Polynomials, Support, Degree, and Polynomial Rings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic objects and descriptors for multivariate polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbb N^n\), the associated monomial is \(x^a=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\). A polynomial over a field \(k\) is a finite sum \(f=\sum_a c_a x^a\), with \(c_a\in k\). Its support is \(\operatorname{supp}(f)=\{a:c_a\ne0\}\), and, for \(f\ne0\), its total degree is \(\deg f=\max_{a\in\operatorname{supp}(f)}\|a\|_1\). For \(k\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), \(k[x]=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is the set of these polynomials equipped with polynomial addition and multiplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multivariate monomial is indexed by a nonnegative-integer exponent vector. A polynomial is a finite scalar linear combination of monomials; its support records the nonzero coefficients, and its total degree is the largest sum of exponents in its support. Over the real or complex field, all such polynomials form a polynomial ring under addition and multiplication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\text{ is the polynomial ring determined by these finite sums and the usual addition and multiplication.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_\alpha x^\alpha\), its Newton polytope is \(\operatorname{Newt}(p)=\operatorname{conv}(A)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F_u=\{\alpha\in\operatorname{Newt}(p):u\cdot\alpha=\max_{\beta\in\operatorname{Newt}(p)}u\cdot\beta\}\) is the exposed face with normal \(u\), then the associated face polynomial is \(p_{F_u}(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A\cap F_u}c_\alpha x^\alpha\). Thus vertices, edges, and higher-dimensional faces encode precisely the monomial groups dominant under corresponding weighted scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Newton polytope is the convex hull of a polynomial's exponent support. Each exposed face determines a face polynomial containing exactly the monomials lying on that face.

children.title: Circuit Supports
children.top_down_role: Polynomial support configurations organized around minimal affine dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex circuits with one relative-interior exponent, as used in sparse polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simplex circuit support is a set \(A=\{\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r),\beta\}\) such that \(\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r)\) are affinely independent and \(\beta\) lies in the relative interior of their convex hull. Equivalently, unique coefficients \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_r>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j=1\) and \(\beta=\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j\alpha(j)\). The set \(A\) is minimally affinely dependent and hence is a circuit of the affine exponent configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex circuit consists of affinely independent outer exponents and one exponent in their relative interior, yielding a unique strictly positive barycentric relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(A=\{\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r),\beta\}\) is a simplex circuit with a unique positive barycentric relation for \(\beta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard simplex-circuit support used in sparse polynomial nonnegativity

children.title: Simplex Supports
children.top_down_role: Polynomial support configurations whose convex hull has simplex geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex supports whose Newton polytope is a simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponent set \(A=\{\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r)\}\) is a simplex support when its points are affinely independent, equivalently when \(\alpha(1)-\alpha(0),\ldots,\alpha(r)-\alpha(0)\) are linearly independent. Its convex hull \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is then an \(r\)-dimensional simplex. Every \(y\in\Delta\) has a unique representation \(y=\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j\alpha(j)\), where \(\lambda_j\ge0\) for every \(j\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^r\lambda_j=1\). If a polynomial has support exactly \(A\), then its Newton polytope is \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex support is an affinely independent exponent set. Its convex hull is a simplex, and every point in that hull has unique barycentric coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is a simplex support exactly when its elements are affinely independent; then \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is an \(r\)-simplex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard affine-geometric definition of a simplex vertex support

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{\alpha_0,ldots,\alpha_r,\beta\}\subseteq A\), with proposed outer simplex \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_r\}\), the support lies on a degenerate boundary if at least one defining circuit condition fails: the vertices \(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_r\) are affinely dependent; \(\beta\notin\operatorname{relint}(\Delta)\); or \(C\) contains a proper affinely dependent subset. The polynomial belongs to the \(t\)-term fewnomial support regime when \(|A|=t\). A family \(\mathcal F\) is support-fewnomial with bound \(t\) when every \(f\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(|\operatorname{supp}(f)|\le t\), even if the ambient dimension or degrees vary. Thus the descriptor records the number and arrangement of nonzero monomials, not merely total degree or coefficient magnitude.

children.title: Variable Block Structure

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A variable block structure is a covering family \(B_1,ldots,B_q\subseteq V\) used to localize polynomial dependence.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not directly define block structures for sparse polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocks may overlap; disjoint blocks are a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A variable block structure on \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a finite family \(\mathcal B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_q\}\) of nonempty subsets satisfying \(\bigcup_{k=1}^{q}B_k=V\). For \(B\subseteq V\), write \(x_B=(x_i)_{i\in B}\). A polynomial \(h\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is supported on block \(B_k\) when \(h\in\mathbb{R}[x_{B_k}]\), equivalently \(\operatorname{var}(h)\subseteq B_k\). The block structure describes which subsets of variables may be treated jointly; it does not require the blocks to be disjoint.

children.title: Correlative Clique Structure
children.top_down_role: Polynomial models organized by cliques in a variable-interaction graph.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correlative cliques are the complete vertex subsets of \(G_{\mathrm{cor}}\), usually chosen maximal for a nonredundant cover.
review_flags: A sparse polynomial-optimization source is needed to confirm the intended clique-completion convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cliques in the original correlative graph; chordal-extension cliques require a separately specified extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_{\mathrm{cor}}=(V,E)\) be the correlative sparsity graph. A set \(C\subseteq V\) is a correlative clique when every pair of distinct indices \(i,j\in C\) satisfies \(\{i,j\}\in E\). It is maximal when no set \(C'\) with \(C\subsetneq C'\subseteq V\) is also a clique. A correlative clique structure is a family \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\}\) of such cliques, commonly the maximal cliques, that covers every vertex and every edge of \(G_{\mathrm{cor}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A correlative clique is a variable subset whose distinct variables are pairwise coupled in the correlative sparsity graph.

children.title: Overlapping Clique Structure
children.top_down_role: Clique organizations with shared variables across local polynomial subsystems.

assumptions_latex: The clique family is \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\}\) with each \(C_k\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The structure is overlapping exactly when some two distinct cliques have a nonempty intersection.

notation.meaning: overlap of cliques indexed by \(k\) and \(\ell\)

review_flags: No supplied source directly treats overlap structure among sparse polynomial cliques.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines overlap and the optional running-intersection consistency condition separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a clique family \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\}\), define the pairwise separator \(S_{k\ell}=C_k\cap C_\ell\). The family has overlapping clique structure when \(S_{k\ell}\ne\varnothing\) for at least one pair \(k\ne\ell\). Given an ordering, it satisfies the running-intersection property when, for every \(k=2,\ldots,q\), there exists \(p(k)<k\) such that \(C_k\cap\bigcup_{j<k}C_j\subseteq C_{p(k)}\). Overlap alone does not imply this property; the latter is an additional consistency condition used to organize shared-variable information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cliques overlap when they share variables; the stronger running-intersection property organizes every accumulated overlap inside one earlier clique.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Clique Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Nonempty pairwise intersection correctly defines the minimal notion of overlapping cliques, but the statement also introduces the running-intersection property, a stronger and distinct structural condition. That addition may exceed this exact leaf, and no source or locator supports either the intended overlap convention or the added condition.

children.title: Block–Clique Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment regimes between prescribed variable blocks and correlative cliques.

assumptions_latex: The variable blocks are \(\mathcal B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_p\}\) and the correlative cliques are \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds when each variable block is contained in a correlative clique.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not establish this block-to-clique compatibility convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses containment compatibility; equality between blocks and cliques is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B=\{B_1,\ldots,B_p\}\) be a variable block structure and \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\}\) a correlative clique structure on the same variable set \(V\). The two structures are block-clique compatible when \[\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\;\exists j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\quad B_k\subseteq C_j.\] Equivalently, every polynomial whose variable set is contained in one prescribed block can be assigned to a clique containing all of its variables. Compatibility permits several blocks within one clique and permits a block to be contained in more than one clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable blocks and correlative cliques are compatible when every block fits wholly inside at least one clique.

assumptions_latex: The variable index set has a partition \(V=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full separability means \(f(x)=c+\sum_{k=1}^{q}f_k(x_{B_k})\) with disjoint variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses additive separability over a partition of the variables.

source_refs.locator: 4.4 DC Representation of Separable Functions p. 110

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_q\) be a partition into nonempty blocks. A polynomial \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is fully separable with respect to this partition when there exist polynomials \(f_k\in\mathbb{R}[x_{B_k}]\) and a constant \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(x)=c+\sum_{k=1}^{q}f_k(x_{B_k})\). Equivalently, every nonconstant monomial of \(f\) involves variables from at most one block. No monomial may simultaneously contain variables indexed by two distinct blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is fully separable when it is a sum of block polynomials over disjoint variable blocks, with no cross-block monomial.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partially separable function and Hessian assembly
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General smooth partially separable structure, not restricted to polynomial functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is partially separable if \(f(x)=\sum_i f_i(A_i x)\), where each \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m_i\times n}\) has few rows. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is partially separable when it is a sum of component functions that each depend on only a few linear combinations of the variables. When the components are twice differentiable, its Hessian is assembled from their low-dimensional Hessians.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes failure relative to a proposed family of variable blocks.

Consequently, its feasible set and objective values are constant on every \(H\)-orbit.

children.title: Sign-Flip Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Polynomial model invariance under selected variable sign changes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is invariant under the sign flip \(s_J\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous invariance of all model polynomials under one coordinate sign flip.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polynomial optimization model has sign-flip symmetry on \(J\) if \(p(s_Jx)=p(x)\) for every \(p\in\{f,g_1,\ldots,g_s\}\) and every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For an individual polynomial \(p(x)=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha x^\alpha\), this is equivalent to \(\sum_{i\in J}\alpha_i\equiv0\pmod 2\) for every \(\alpha\in\operatorname{supp}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign-flip symmetry negates selected coordinates without changing any model polynomial; equivalently, every active monomial has even total exponent on those coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Flip Symmetry

children.title: Exponent-Parity Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Support patterns organized by parity classes of monomial exponents.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_p\) is the exponent-parity structure of \(p\).

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise reduction of an exponent vector modulo two.
Set of parity vectors of active monomials.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity data of active exponent vectors, viewed over \(\mathbb{F}_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponent-parity structure of \(p\) is \(P_p=\{\alpha\bmod2:p_\alpha\ne0\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n\). If \(u\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\) encodes the sign change \(x_i\mapsto(-1)^{u_i}x_i\), then the monomial \(x^\alpha\) is multiplied by \((-1)^{u^\mathsf{T}\bar\alpha}\). Hence \(p\) is invariant under this sign change exactly when \(u^\mathsf{T}v=0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_2\) for every \(v\in P_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent parity reduces each active monomial's exponent vector modulo two and thereby determines exactly which coordinate sign changes preserve the polynomial.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponent-Parity Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity-support representation correctly captures sign invariance and fits the leaf, but it lacks a source with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model's sign-parity interaction regime is determined by \(L^\perp\), where \(L=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(P)\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal complement over the binary field.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary orthogonality links exponent patterns to the model's sign-symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encode a coordinate sign change by \(u\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\), acting as \(x_i\mapsto(-1)^{u_i}x_i\). The change preserves every \(p_k\) if and only if \(u^\mathsf{T}v=0\) for every \(v\in P\). Therefore the admissible sign changes are exactly \(L^\perp\). The regimes range from full sign symmetry when \(L=\{0\}\), through intermediate symmetry when \(0<\dim L<n\), to no nontrivial sign symmetry when \(L=\mathbb{F}_2^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The span of all active exponent parities and its binary orthogonal complement classify full, partial, and trivial model-level sign symmetry.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign–Parity Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary orthogonality duality is internally consistent and correctly distinguishes full, intermediate, and trivial sign symmetry, but no supporting citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proposed sign symmetry is broken by the model.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sign symmetry encoded by \(u\) is broken if and only if some model polynomial \(p_k\) contains an active monomial \((p_k)_\alpha x^\alpha\) with \(u^\mathsf{T}\bar\alpha=1\) in \(\mathbb{F}_2\). Under the associated coordinate sign change, that monomial changes sign. Since distinct monomials are linearly independent, \(p_k\) is not invariant, and consequently the full polynomial optimization model lacks the proposed symmetry.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial model is group-invariant when a linear group action preserves every displayed constraint polynomial and the objective, hence preserves feasibility and objective values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The presentation \(K=\{x:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,s\}\) is Archimedean when there exists \(R>0\) such that \(R-\lVert x\rVert_2^2\in M(g)\). Explicitly, this means \(R-\lVert x\rVert_2^2=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^s\sigma_jg_j\) for sums-of-squares polynomials \(\sigma_j\). Evaluating on \(K\) gives \(\lVert x\rVert_2^2\le R\); hence \(K\) is bounded and, being closed, compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A presentation is Archimedean when its quadratic module certifies a ball bound; this certificate makes the basic closed feasible set compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A compact real algebraic variety is a set \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_i(x)=0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}\) that is compact in the Euclidean topology. Since every polynomial zero set is closed, compactness is equivalent to boundedness. If \(V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)\ne\varnothing\), each polynomial \(f\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) attains both \(\min_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x)\) and \(\max_{x\in V_{\mathbb{R}}(h)}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact real algebraic variety is a bounded common real zero set of finitely many polynomials; polynomial objectives attain their extrema on every nonempty such set.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Smooth Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact polynomial equality loci for which zero is a regular value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_1(x)=\cdots=h_r(x)=0\}\). If \(M\) is nonempty and compact and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=r\) for every \(x\in M\), then \(0\in\mathbb{R}^r\) is a regular value of \(h\), so \(M\) is a compact smooth embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) of dimension \(n-r\). At every \(x\in M\), its tangent space is \(T_xM=\ker Dh(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty compact polynomial equality locus is a compact smooth embedded manifold of dimension n minus r when the defining Jacobian has full row rank r at every point of the locus; its tangent space is the Jacobian kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a compact smooth embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) of dimension \(n-r\), with \(T_xM=\ker Dh(x)\) for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of h at x.
Tangent space at x under the regular-value hypothesis.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Compact Varieties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-dimensional compact real algebraic varieties having at least one Jacobian-singular point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\in\mathbb R[x]^m\) and \(V=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h(x)=0\}\). Assume that \(V\) is nonempty, compact, and pure-dimensional of dimension \(d\). The variety \(V\) is singular when its singular locus \[\operatorname{Sing}(V)=\{x\in V:\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)<n-d\}\] is nonempty. A polynomial optimization problem \(\inf_{x\in V}f(x)\), with \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\), is then a singular compact-variety model; compactness guarantees attainment despite the singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact pure-dimensional algebraic feasible set is singular if its defining Jacobian loses the expected rank somewhere; every polynomial objective still attains its minimum on it.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is nonempty, compact, and pure-dimensional of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sing}(V)\ne\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in V}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of the defining polynomial map
real dimension of the pure-dimensional variety

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold-Constrained Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained polynomial optimization on a compact smooth real algebraic manifold defined by a regular polynomial level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\leq n\), let \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_m):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be polynomial, and set \(M=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h(x)=0\}\). A manifold-constrained polynomial model is \[f^*=\min_{x\in M}f(x),\qquad f\in\mathbb R[x],\] where \(M\) is nonempty and compact and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=m\) for every \(x\in M\). Then \(M\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(d=n-m\), and the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes a polynomial over a nonempty compact polynomial equality set at which the equality Jacobian has full row rank; the feasible set is a smooth manifold of dimension n-m and the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(n-m\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in M}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of the polynomial equality map

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Noncompact Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment for polynomial objectives coercive relative to a closed noncompact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and noncompact, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The objective is coercive on \(K\) when \[\lim_{\substack{x\in K\\ \|x\|\to\infty}}f(x)=+\infty.\] Every sublevel set \(\{x\in K:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is then compact. Consequently, \(f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\) is finite and is attained by at least one point of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed noncompact feasible set, a polynomial growing to positive infinity along every escaping feasible sequence has compact sublevels and attains a finite minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*>-\infty\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: global infimum of the objective over the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Noncoercive Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact polynomial models whose minimum exists without relative coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and noncompact, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The model is attained but noncoercive when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R,\qquad \{x\in K:f(x)=f^*\}\ne\varnothing,\] while there exists a sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) such that \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) and \(f(x_k)\not\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polynomial has a finite global minimizer on a closed noncompact feasible set, although some feasible sequence escapes to infinity without the objective tending to positive infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\ne\varnothing\), but \(f\) is not coercive on \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment at Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite infimum approached only by feasible sequences escaping every bounded region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). Nonattainment at infinity occurs when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R,\qquad \{x\in K:f(x)=f^*\}=\varnothing.\] Every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) satisfying \(f(x_k)\to f^*\) then satisfies \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum is finite but no feasible point realizes it; because the feasible set is closed, every minimizing sequence must escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) satisfies \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Polynomial Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial minimization models whose objective is unbounded below on the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty basic semialgebraic set and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The minimization model is unbounded below when \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty.\] Equivalently, for every \(M\in\mathbb R\) there exists \(x_M\in K\) such that \(f(x_M)<M\). Thus the model has neither a finite optimal value nor a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial minimization model is unbounded below when feasible objective values fall below every real threshold, so no finite optimum or minimizer exists.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and basic semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty semialgebraic set and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Dimensional Feasible Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial optimization over zero-dimensional semialgebraic feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty semialgebraic set and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). If \(\dim K=0\), then \(K\) is finite. Hence \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=\min_{x\in K}f(x),\] and the set of global minimizers is a nonempty finite subset of \(K\). Thus zero-dimensional feasible models reduce mathematically to comparison over finitely many feasible points, although enumerating those points may remain difficult.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty zero-dimensional semialgebraic feasible set is finite, so every polynomial objective attains its minimum by finite comparison.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The optimal value is attained when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R\quad\text{and}\quad \exists x^*\in K\;\; f(x^*)=f^*.\] Equivalently, the global solution set \(K^*=\{x\in K:f(x)=f^*\}\) is nonempty. Attainment is distinct from merely having a finite infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal value is attained when the finite infimum equals the objective value at at least one feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moment formula for the best polynomial approximation of an optimizer coordinate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The optimizer mapping is considered under the unexpanded hypotheses referenced by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 14.5. Let \(g_k\in L_2(\varphi)\) be the \(k\)-th coordinate of the global-minimizer mapping, let \(M_d(\varphi)\) be the order-\(d\) moment matrix, and define \(u^d_\beta=\int_{\mathbf Y}\mathbf y^\beta g_k(\mathbf y)\,d\varphi(\mathbf y)\) for \(\beta\in\mathbb N_d^p\). If \(M_d(\varphi)\) is invertible and the degree-\(d\) polynomial \(p_d^*\) has coefficient vector \(\mathbf p_d^*=M_d(\varphi)^{-1}\mathbf u^d\), then \(p_d^*\) is a best degree-\(d\) approximation to \(g_k\) in \(L_2(\varphi)\). In the orthonormal-polynomial basis associated with \(\varphi\), its coefficients are the corresponding generalized moments \(\mathbf u^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best degree-d least-squares polynomial approximation of an optimizer-map coordinate is obtained by solving the moment-matrix normal equations. In the associated orthonormal polynomial basis, the approximation coefficients are the generalized moments of that coordinate.
assumptions_latex: u^d_\beta=\int_{\mathbf Y}\mathbf y^\beta g_k(\mathbf y)\,d\varphi(\mathbf y)\quad(\beta\in\mathbb N_d^p).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf p_d^*=M_d(\varphi)^{-1}\mathbf u^d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\int_{\mathbf Y}(p_d^*-g_k)^2\,d\varphi=\inf_{p\in\mathbb R[\mathbf y]_d}\int_{\mathbf Y}(p-g_k)^2\,d\varphi;\quad\text{in the associated orthonormal basis, the coefficients are }\mathbf u^d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery of binary optimizer-coordinate probabilities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The result is conditional on the unexpanded convergence hypotheses referenced by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses guaranteeing the parametric moment--SDP convergence used in Theorem 14.5, and let \((\mathbf z^d)\) be nearly optimal solutions of relaxations (14.14). For fixed \(k\in I\), if every optimal solution satisfies \(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1\) (respectively, \(0\)) for \(\varphi\)-almost every \(\mathbf y\in\mathbf Y\), then \(\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0}=1\) (respectively, \(0\)). If, additionally, the optimal solution \(\mathbf x^*(\mathbf y)\) is unique for \(\varphi\)-almost every \(\mathbf y\), then \(\operatorname{Prob}_{\mathbf y\sim\varphi}(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1)=\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0}\). Consequently, \(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1\) (respectively, \(0\)) almost everywhere if and only if this limit equals \(1\) (respectively, \(0\)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the assumed moment–SDP convergence conditions, an optimizer coordinate that is always 1 or always 0 almost everywhere forces the corresponding limiting relaxation moment to equal that value. When the optimizer is almost everywhere unique, the limiting moment equals the probability that the coordinate is 1, yielding an if-and-only-if criterion for an almost-surely fixed binary coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \text{The parametric moment--SDP convergence hypotheses referenced in Theorem 14.5 hold.}
\mathbf z^d\text{ is nearly optimal for relaxation (14.14) for each }d.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[x_k^*(\mathbf y)=b\ \varphi\text{-a.e. for every optimizer}\bigr]\Rightarrow\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0}=b\quad(b\in\{0,1\});\quad\text{under a.e. uniqueness, }\operatorname{Prob}(x_k^*(\mathbf y)=1)=\lim_{d\to\infty}z^d_{e(k)0},\text{ and the implication becomes an equivalence for }b\in\{0,1\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Hypersurface Representation of the Optimal-Value Polynomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective-dual characterization for linear optimization over a smooth, compact, irreducible real affine variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subset\mathbb R^n be an irreducible, smooth, compact real affine variety, and let X^*\subset(\mathbb P^n)^* be the dual variety of its projective closure. Then X^* is an irreducible hypersurface. If \Phi(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_n) represents the optimal-value function of (5.26) as in \Phi(c_0^*,c_1,\ldots,c_n)=0, then a defining polynomial of X^* is \Phi(-c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_n). Consequently, if F defines X^*, then the algebraic degree of (5.26) is \deg_{c_0}F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth, compact, irreducible real affine variety, the dual of its projective closure is an irreducible hypersurface. Its equation is the optimal-value polynomial with the value coordinate negated, and its degree in that coordinate is the algebraic degree of the optimization problem.
assumptions_latex: X\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is an irreducible, smooth, compact real affine variety}
X^*\subset(\mathbb P^n)^*\text{ is the dual of the projective closure of }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X^*\text{ is an irreducible hypersurface defined by }\Phi(-c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_n),\qquad \operatorname{algdeg}(5.26)=\deg_{c_0}F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Optimal-Value Function and Algebraic Degree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The unambiguous algebraic-value claims for objective-parametric linear optimization over a fixed compact real algebraic variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varnothing\ne X=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h_1(x)=\cdots=h_p(x)=0\} be compact and define v(c)=\min_{x\in X}\langle c,x\rangle. Then v(c) is finite and attained for every c\in\mathbb R^n. There exists a nonzero polynomial \Phi(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_n) such that \Phi(v(c),c_1,\ldots,c_n)=0 for all c. For a least-degree polynomial relation \Phi as specified in the source, \deg_{c_0}\Phi is called the algebraic degree of the optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty compact real algebraic variety, every linear objective has an attained finite minimum. The resulting value function satisfies a polynomial equation, and the degree of a least-degree value polynomial in the value coordinate is called the algebraic degree of the problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall c\in\mathbb R^n,\ v(c)\in\mathbb R\text{ is attained},\qquad \Phi(v(c),c)=0,\qquad \operatorname{algdeg}=\deg_{c_0}\Phi.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Finite Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial models with a finite infimum but an empty global solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). The model has a nonattained finite infimum when \[f^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb R\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(x_\varepsilon\in K\) with \(f(x_\varepsilon)<f^*+\varepsilon\), but no feasible point has objective value \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is bounded below and can approach a finite infimum arbitrarily closely, but no feasible point realizes that value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polynomial minimization problem is in an unbounded-objective regime precisely when, for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\), there exists \(x_M\in K\) such that \(f(x_M)<M\). Equivalently, there is a sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq1}\subseteq K\) satisfying \(f(x_k)\to-\infty\). Thus the problem has no finite optimal value and no global minimizer with real objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization problem is objective-unbounded when feasible points attain arbitrarily negative objective values, equivalently when its infimum is negative infinity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness concerns objective values escaping every finite bound in the optimizing direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear programming model with feasible region F and objective f is unbounded if, for maximization, f(x) can be made arbitrarily large over x\in F, or, for minimization, f(x) can be made arbitrarily small over x\in F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear programming model is unbounded when feasible objective values can be made arbitrarily large in maximization or arbitrarily small in minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in F}f(x)=+\infty\text{ for maximization, or }\inf_{x\in F}f(x)=-\infty\text{ for minimization}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is specified entirely by finitely many polynomials in \(\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a real polynomial optimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimization models over real affine coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real polynomial coordinate model is an optimization problem of the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\geq0\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad h_j(x)=0\ \ (j=1,\ldots,r),\] where \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m,h_1,\ldots,h_r\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Its feasible set is the basic closed semialgebraic set \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real polynomial coordinate model optimizes a real polynomial over real coordinates subject to finitely many real polynomial inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Real Polynomial Coordinate Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard and fits the container, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Complex Polynomial Models
children.top_down_role: Polynomial model families expressed directly in complex coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All model functions belong to \(\mathbb{C}[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard holomorphic polynomial coordinate model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Holomorphic polynomial models; real-valued Hermitian models are treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complex polynomial model is a finite system \[p_i(z)=0\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad q_j(z)\neq0\ \ (j=1,\ldots,r),\] or an optimization model built from such functions, where \(z\in\mathbb{C}^n\) and every \(p_i,q_j\) lies in \(\mathbb{C}[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\). Dependence is polynomial in \(z\) alone; conjugate variables \(\bar z\) do not occur. An order-valued objective requires an explicitly real-valued scalarization because \(\mathbb{C}\) has no compatible total order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complex polynomial model uses holomorphic polynomials in complex coordinates; optimization requires a separately specified real-valued objective or scalarization.
knowledge_statements.title: Complex Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The holomorphic model distinction is plausible, but the inclusion of inequations and real-valued scalarization conventions requires an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hilbert Nullstellensatz Infeasibility Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex polynomial equation systems and ideal-membership infeasibility certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,\ldots,z_n]$, the system $f_i(z)=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$ has no solution in $\mathbb{C}^n$ if and only if $-1\in\langle f_1,\ldots,f_m\rangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite system of complex polynomial equations is infeasible over complex space exactly when minus one belongs to the ideal generated by those polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{z\in\mathbb{C}^n:f_i(z)=0\ \forall i\}=\varnothing\iff -1\in\langle f_1,\ldots,f_m\rangle

children.title: Hermitian Polynomial Models
children.top_down_role: Complex polynomial models organized by Hermitian coefficient or variable structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective and ordered constraints are real-valued polynomials in \((z,\bar z)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: coefficient characterization of real-valued Hermitian polynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued mixed polynomials on complex coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Hermitian polynomial is a finite expression \[p(z,\bar z)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha\beta}z^\alpha\bar z^\beta\] whose coefficients satisfy \(c_{\alpha\beta}=\overline{c_{\beta\alpha}}\). Consequently \(p(z,\bar z)=\overline{p(z,\bar z)}\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}^n\). A Hermitian polynomial optimization model minimizes such an objective subject to inequalities and equalities defined by Hermitian polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hermitian polynomial model uses mixed polynomials in complex variables and their conjugates whose coefficient symmetry makes every ordered model function real-valued.
knowledge_statements.title: Hermitian Polynomial Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hermitian coefficient condition and real-valuedness claim are standard and appropriately classified as a definition, but no inspectable citation is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Archimedeanity and Hermitian-square positivity modulo an ideal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between an Archimedean semiring condition and universal strict-positivity representation on a real variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\triangleleft\mathbb R[x,y]\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(V_{\mathbb R}(I)\) is compact and every \(f\in\mathbb R[x,y]\) satisfying \(f>0\) on \(V_{\mathbb R}(I)\) belongs to \(\Sigma_h+I\); (ii) \(\Sigma_h\) is Archimedean modulo \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real polynomial ideal, Archimedeanity of the Hermitian-square semiring modulo the ideal is equivalent to compactness of the real variety together with representation modulo the ideal of every polynomial strictly positive on that variety.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[V_{\mathbb R}(I)\text{ compact and }(\forall f\in\mathbb R[x,y])\,(f>0\text{ on }V_{\mathbb R}(I)\Rightarrow f\in\Sigma_h+I)\bigr]\iff\Sigma_h\text{ is Archimedean modulo }I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Ratio Criterion for Hermitian Quotients of Square Norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes quotient-of-square-norm representability through a uniform bound away from the polynomial's zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P(z,\bar z)$ be a Hermitian bihomogeneous polynomial on $\mathbb C^d$ with a decomposition $P(z,\bar z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|p_j(z)|^2-\sum_{j=n+1}^{N}|p_j(z)|^2$, where the $p_j$ are linearly independent, and let $V(P)=\{z\in\mathbb C^d:P(z,\bar z)=0\}$. Then $P$ is a quotient of squared polynomial norms if and only if $\sup_{z\notin V(P)}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}|p_j(z)|^2+\sum_{j=n+1}^{N}|p_j(z)|^2}{P(z,\bar z)}<\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Hermitian bihomogeneous polynomial expressed as a difference of squared norms of linearly independent polynomials, quotient-of-squared-norm representability is equivalent to boundedness of the ratio of the corresponding total squared norm to P outside the zero set of P.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is Hermitian and bihomogeneous on }\mathbb C^d
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is a quotient of squared polynomial norms}\iff\sup_{z\notin V(P)}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}|p_j(z)|^2+\sum_{j=n+1}^{N}|p_j(z)|^2}{P(z,\bar z)}<\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hermitian-square representation on the unit sphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict positivity on the real unit sphere in complex coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=x+iy\in\mathbb C^d\) and let \(p\in\mathbb R[x,y]\) satisfy \(p(x,y)>0\) whenever \(\|z\|^2=1\). Then there exist \(n\ge 1\), \(q_1,\ldots,q_n\in\mathbb C[z]\), and \(h\in\mathbb R[x,y]\) such that \[p(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^n|q_j(z)|^2+(1-\|z\|^2)h(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real polynomial strictly positive on the unit sphere is, modulo the sphere equation, a finite sum of squared moduli of complex holomorphic polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists n\ge1,\ q_j\in\mathbb C[z],\ h\in\mathbb R[x,y]:\ p=\sum_{j=1}^n|q_j|^2+(1-\|z\|^2)h

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Univariate Quotient-of-Squared-Norms Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes nonzero real-valued polynomials in one complex variable admitting finite squared-norm quotient representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero real-valued polynomial $P(z,\bar z)$ can be represented as $P(z,\bar z)=\frac{\sum_j|p_j(z)|^2}{\sum_k|q_k(z)|^2}$ with finitely many $p_j,q_k\in\mathbb C[z]$ if and only if there exist finitely many $a_\ell\in\mathbb C$, nonzero integers $n_\ell$, and a polynomial $Q(z,\bar z)$ such that $P(z,\bar z)=\prod_\ell|z-a_\ell|^{2n_\ell}Q(z,\bar z)$ for $z\in\mathbb C$, $Q(z,\bar z)>0$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$, and $2\deg_zQ=\deg Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero real-valued polynomial in one complex variable is a quotient of finite sums of squared polynomial moduli exactly when it has the stated squared-distance factorization with an everywhere-positive residual polynomial satisfying the degree condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\frac{\sum_j|p_j|^2}{\sum_k|q_k|^2}\iff\exists\,a_\ell\in\mathbb C,\ n_\ell\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\},\ Q:\ P=\prod_\ell|z-a_\ell|^{2n_\ell}Q,\ Q>0,\ 2\deg_zQ=\deg Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Free *-algebra, analytic elements, and hereditary elements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the ambient involutive algebra and two distinguished classes of its elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\mathbb R\langle x_1,\ldots,x_d,x_1^*,\ldots,x_d^*\rangle\) be the free real algebra with an \(\mathbb R\)-linear involution satisfying \((fg)^*=g^*f^*\), \((x_k)^*=x_k^*\), and \((x_k^*)^*=x_k\). An element \(f\in\mathcal A\) is analytic when \(f\in\mathbb R\langle x_1,\ldots,x_d\rangle\). It is hereditary when, in every monomial of \(f\), every starred generator occurs to the left of every unstarred generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The free real algebra on generators and their formal adjoints carries the order-reversing involution. An element is analytic if it uses only the unstarred generators, and hereditary if each of its monomials places all starred generators before all unstarred generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is analytic}\iff f\in\mathbb R\langle x_1,\ldots,x_d\rangle;\qquad f\text{ is hereditary}\iff\text{ every word of }f\text{ has all }x_k^*\text{ before all }x_j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quillen's Hermitian-square certificate theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires strict positivity at every nonzero complex vector and uses a positive integral power of the squared Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(z,\bar z)\) be a bihomogeneous form on \(\mathbb C^d\). If \(f(z,\bar z)>0\) for every \(z\neq0\), then there exists \(N\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) such that \(\lVert z\rVert^{2N}f(z,\bar z)\) is a sum of Hermitian squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bihomogeneous form that is strictly positive at all nonzero points of complex space becomes a sum of Hermitian squares after multiplication by a sufficiently high positive integral power of the squared Euclidean norm.
assumptions_latex: f(z,\bar z)\text{ is a bihomogeneous form on }\mathbb C^d
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists N\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\text{ such that }\lVert z\rVert^{2N}f(z,\bar z)\text{ is a sum of Hermitian squares}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hereditary free-algebra positivity certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The constraint index is understood to range over all listed analytic elements \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\); the source notation \(\operatorname{sym}(p)\) is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\in\mathcal A\) be analytic and let \(q=q^*\in\mathcal A\) be hereditary. If, for every finite-dimensional matrix tuple \(X\) and vector \(v\) satisfying \(p_j(X)v=0\) for all \(j=1,\ldots,m\), one has \(\langle q(X)v,v\rangle\ge 0\), then there exist finitely many analytic \(f_k\in\mathcal A\) and \(g\in\operatorname{sym}(p)\) such that \(q=\sum_k f_k^*f_k+g\). If instead \(\langle q(X)v,v\rangle=0\) for every such pair \((X,v)\), then \(q\in\operatorname{sym}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric hereditary free polynomial that is nonnegative on every finite-dimensional vector satisfying the analytic constraints is a finite sum of analytic Hermitian squares modulo the associated symmetric constraint space. If it vanishes on every such constrained vector, it belongs to that constraint space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall(X,v),\ \langle q(X)v,v\rangle\ge0\bigr]\Rightarrow q=\sum_k f_k^*f_k+g,\quad f_k\text{ analytic},\ g\in\operatorname{sym}(p);\qquad \bigl[\forall(X,v),\ \langle q(X)v,v\rangle=0\bigr]\Rightarrow q\in\operatorname{sym}(p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hermitian-square positivity on coercive hypersurfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict positivity representation on hypersurfaces defined by a norm plus Hermitian squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[H=\left\{z\in\mathbb C^d:\ \|z\|^2+\sum_{k=1}^{r}|q_k(z)|^2=M\right\},\] where \(q_k\in\mathbb C[z]\) and \(M>0\). Every real polynomial that is strictly positive on \(H\) is, as a polynomial function on \(H\), a finite sum of Hermitian squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a real hypersurface defined by the squared norm plus finitely many Hermitian squares equaling a positive constant, every strictly positive polynomial function is a sum of Hermitian squares on that hypersurface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists s_1,\ldots,s_n\in\mathbb C[z]\text{ such that }p(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|s_j(z)|^2\quad\text{for all }z\in H

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hermite root-counting theorem for the associated Hermitian form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts roots in the two open half-planes and roots shared with the conjugate polynomial using the inertia of the associated Hermitian form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb C[\zeta]\) have degree \(n\), and let \(H_p\) be its associated Hermitian form. If \(n_+(H_p)\) and \(n_-(H_p)\) are respectively the numbers of positive and negative squares in a diagonal decomposition of \(H_p\), then \(p\) has \(n_+(H_p)\) roots in \(\{\operatorname{Im}\zeta>0\}\), \(n_-(H_p)\) roots in \(\{\operatorname{Im}\zeta<0\}\), and \(n-n_+(H_p)-n_-(H_p)\) roots common to \(p\) and \(p^*\), namely real roots or roots occurring with their complex conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a degree-n complex polynomial, the positive and negative indices of its associated Hermitian form count its roots in the upper and lower half-planes; the remaining count consists of roots common to the polynomial and its conjugate polynomial, including real roots and conjugate-paired roots.
assumptions_latex: H_p\text{ is the Hermitian form associated with }p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\operatorname{Im}\zeta>0}(p)=n_+(H_p),\quad N_{\operatorname{Im}\zeta<0}(p)=n_-(H_p),\quad N_{\mathrm{common}}(p,p^*)=n-n_+(H_p)-n_-(H_p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schur root-counting theorem for the associated form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts roots inside and outside the unit circle using the signature of the polynomial's associated form, while retaining the exceptional unit-circle or circle-conjugate cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb C[\zeta]\) have degree \(n\), associated form \(S_p\), and signature indices \(n_+(S_p)\) and \(n_-(S_p)\). Then \(p\) has \(n_+(S_p)\) roots in \(\{|\zeta|<1\}\), \(n_-(S_p)\) roots in \(\{|\zeta|>1\}\), and \(n-n_+(S_p)-n_-(S_p)\) roots of modulus one or conjugated with respect to the unit circle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive and negative signature indices of the associated form count a degree-n polynomial's roots inside the open unit disk and outside the closed unit disk. The remaining count comprises roots on the unit circle or roots conjugated with respect to that circle.
assumptions_latex: S_p\text{ is the form associated with }p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{|\zeta|<1}(p)=n_+(S_p),\quad N_{|\zeta|>1}(p)=n_-(S_p),\quad N_{\mathrm{unit\text{-}circle\ or\ circle\text{-}conjugate}}=n-n_+(S_p)-n_-(S_p).
